chapters.title: The End of a Long Sleep
paragraphs: I found everything to be new to me. The apple trees were laden with enormous fruits, and the orchard stretched upwards along the mountain’s height, reaching all the way to the summit. Here and there, pipes and channels had been installed to carry away the rainwater. Thick pipes distributed water everywhere. In some places, taps for drinking water could also be seen. A little off the path, a few small tin houses seemed to stand, but I did not wish to leave the road to go there. I thought, let me keep going ahead; surely, somewhere along the way, I will meet someone.

After walking a full four kos, at last I heard human voices. The closer I drew, the clearer the sounds became. When I reached them, I saw that both men and women were present. Their garments were exceedingly clean; their faces radiant. I wondered to myself, could these be members of the royal family of Nepal, perhaps come here for amusement? But it did not seem so. They were picking fruits, placing them in baskets, and setting them on the ground, while some others carried those very fruits away before them. It appeared they must be piling them up somewhere. Besides, the women did not wear the twenty-yard pajamas of the royal household; though their complexion, attire, physical build, cleanliness, and manners were of a far higher order, there was certainly a difference. All of them wore pants; their hands and feet were covered with gloves and socks. They wore shoes as well. There must be some mystery in this. Well, I shall find out by meeting them. And now, I was quite close. Because they were absorbed in their work, they did not notice me. But look, over there—one of them, having seen me, said something to his companions. Are they all staring at me, eyes wide open? Am I some kind of creature? Some are looking at my leafy clothes, others at my beard. Ah, one man is coming this way; from him, I shall learn everything.
Although the man approaching was coming straight towards me, my curiosity made me impatient.

chapters.title: The Orchards of Sebgram
paragraphs: That man slowly approached me and said, “Welcome.” Though he uttered this word only once, it seemed to echo in my ears countless times. Only after this did our conversation begin—
“Where have you come from?”
“Not from very far; it was about two hours after sunrise when I set out from my place.”
“Now,”—glancing quickly at his watch—“it is already twenty minutes past three. Forgive me if my words seem somewhat bold, for the very sight of you has stirred waves of curiosity in my heart.”

“Say whatever you wish, without hesitation. My own curiosity is no less than yours. Although my dwelling is not far from this place, I am certainly far from it in terms of time. Well, tell me, what year is it today?”
“The year 100.”
“Which year?”
“Universal. Which year do you mean?”
“The Christian era.”
“That would be 2124.”
“Oh-ho! So I have been sitting in the cave for two hundred years? No wonder I see nothing but change everywhere. Well, ask whatever you wish to ask.”
“Have you really been sitting in the cave for two hundred years? And how old were you when you entered?”
“Sixty years.”
“Two hundred and sixty years is a great age. I myself am sixty years old. In Vriddhapur there are several men between a hundred and a hundred and twenty years old. But your age—”

So far, I have not heard a single man’s voice. All these things are filling me with even greater wonder; at the same time, a strong curiosity to ask many questions is welling up within me. However, the women and men who are my companions here are no less curious than I am. Therefore, how wonderful it would be if you were to tell your life story in their presence.
x x x
Yes, one more thing. Such garments are no longer in fashion; it would not be improper, would it, if I were to bring you some clothes to wear?”
“No, not at all. In fact, I too have felt the need for them.”

As soon as I finished my sentence, that gentleman called out, “Arjun! Arjun!” and at the sound of his voice, a young man came running. With a smiling face, he welcomed me and asked his companion, “What is it?”
“There must be some dhotis and garments kept in this house. Please run and bring one of them here… for you to wear.”
“Very well,” said Arjun, and he dashed off, returning in two minutes with an impeccably clean dhoti.
Taking the dhoti, I said, “First of all, since we have much to discuss, we should become acquainted by name. My name is Vishwabandhu, and may I know your name?”
“My name is Sumedh.”
“So, Sumedh ji! Thank you for your assistance.”

“No, it is nothing. Now it is time for us to have refreshments. You must be tired and weary—it is only natural that you would be hungry as well. Let us go and have some refreshments, and afterwards, please grace us with your life story.”
“Sumedh! Truly, your few words of conversation have greatly attracted me. At this moment, my joy knows no bounds. Very well, let us go.”
Now Sumedh led me towards that house. Just then, suddenly, there was a sound like the firing of a cannon. At first, I was startled, but upon asking…

It seemed this was the signal for refreshments. One more curiosity was added to my many questions. I saw that the men and women who had been working also left their tasks and began walking toward this building. As I approached the house, what did I see? Numerous taps of clear water were installed. There were tubs of clean water for bathing. The building itself was very neat. There were three or four large rooms. One hall was big enough to seat a hundred and fifty to two hundred people. The rooms were filled with many chairs.

In the large hall, I saw rows of chairs and tables arranged. On each table, in a plate, there were apples, bananas, grapes, and many other fruits, and glasses filled with milk. Our group of men and women numbered about a hundred. At first, I was surprised to see exactly that many plates there. Would the women also sit beside the men and take breakfast together? Just then, all the men and women arrived. All greeted me with smiling faces. Addressing them, Mr. Sumedh said—

“Friends, everyone is very curious to see our guest today. And as for those like us—who have already heard a thing or two—our eagerness knows no bounds. That is why I thought it best not to hear everything alone. So far, all I know is that our Vishvabandhuji has been settled since 1624, just ten or twelve kos from here, from where he has come today.”

Hearing this, the curiosity of the men and women grew even more intense, but the time for refreshments was passing. So, everyone washed their hands and faces and took their seats. Needless to say, Arjun had already told me, while taking away my dhoti, that he would serve my breakfast plate. Sumedh seated me on a chair and sat down beside me himself. Close to him sat a lady, whom I later learned was his companion, Sumitra. The servers, having finished their work, also took their seats. Now everyone began their breakfast. I too put a slice of apple in my mouth. Its sweetness and juiciness seemed extraordinary to me. At that moment, I thought perhaps it tasted so delicious because I was eating after such a long time.

chapters.title: The Present World
paragraphs: It seemed so, but later I learned that this was the result of scientific methods of fruit cultivation. Mistaking me for someone especially hungry, they had given me a little more fruit. Among them were also some segments of orange. I had tasted oranges from Nepal before, but never were they so sweet and delicious. There was no trace of seeds, nor any fibers. The grapes were the size of Banarasi berries. I asked,
"Where are these grapes from?"
Sumedh replied, "There is an orchard four kos from here."
"Do grapes grow in Nepal as well?"
"Very much so. It's been hundreds of years now. Grapes from here are sent to all of Bihar, Orissa, half of Bengal, Kashi, and Kosala."

Now breakfast was over. Everyone washed their hands and faces and turned toward a room. There, many kurtas were lying about. Sumedh took me and seated me on a comfortable chair. Inwardly, I kept thinking that these people must surely consider me a savage from the twentieth century. And on top of that, they had seen me clad in leaves! Besides, none of them seemed fond of beards, while my hair was like that of a bear!
I had seen these people working in the orchard, so I had assumed they must be laborers. But now I was curious to ask, who owns these orchards? Yet I did not have the courage.
"We are all very eager to hear your story."

"I am even more eager to learn about you than you are about me. Sumedhji, my story is not very long. Before coming to that cave, I lived in Nalanda, in the province of Bihar. At that time, there was a school there, where I used to study and teach."

“Oh! You are Vishvabandhu, the teacher of Nalanda University? Truly, how fortunate we are to behold you! I, too, was nurtured in the lap of your very university from the age of three until twenty. In the ‘Vasubandhu Hall’ there, I have even seen your stone statue!”
“So, our beloved university still lives?”
“Not only does it live, but today there is perhaps no other institution in the world that can rival it. In philosophy, astronomy, linguistics, history, and politics, Nalanda is unparalleled.”

As I listened to the account of Nalanda University’s glory, my joy knew no bounds; a sea of delight surged within my heart. The audience, too, seemed deeply moved by this introduction. All of them gazed at me with such looks, filled with affection and respect. Now, they had learned all that was to be known about me. To learn about them, I quickly brought my own story to a close—

“After serving the university for nearly thirty years, I set out to wander in the northern regions. Upon reaching that cave, which lies twelve or thirteen kos from here, I fell into a swoon or sleep, and have lain there ever since. That, in brief, is my story. Now, tell me—where is your birthplace? Your language does not seem to be Nepali?”

“That Nepali tongue, you will not hear spoken anywhere now. Yes, in libraries, its books may still be found. But now, throughout all of India, only one language is spoken. None of us were born in the same place. Though my father was born in Kathmandu, after completing his education at Nalanda University, he made Shak-gram in Gaya district his field of work. I was born there. My father is still alive, and nowadays lives with my mother in the Elderly Village of Hazaribagh. He is over a hundred years old. The same is true for all our companions here. My companion Sumitra”—[pointing to the woman seated nearby]—“was born in Kashi.

However, their education too was at the Nalanda School. After marriage, both of us decided to work here. My companion Arjun was born in Anuradhapura, Lanka, but when he was only a year old, his parents settled in Bodh Gaya, and he too received his education at Nalanda. His partner, Pratibha, is from Kashmir, yet her education was at the same school. In this way, all the companions present here—there are a hundred of them—their birthplaces are scarcely fewer than a hundred. In our Sevagram, the population is five thousand, of which half the men and women are from other places. The fact is, at the age of three, boys go to school for their education, and when their studies end at the age of twenty, very few of them return to their native villages. Each one, according to the knowledge and craft that interests him, settles in a community suited to that pursuit.
“So it seems that now, in every matter, there is a difference from the olden times. Well then, tell me, who is the king of Nepal at present?”
“The king of Nepal! The word ‘king’ now only graces the pages of books. Where are there kings now?”
“Well then, whose are these gardens?”
“Now everything belongs to the nation, not just the gardens. This house, these chairs, beds, children, men and women—all belong to the nation.”
“Then how is the nation governed?”
“By the councils of elders elected by us. The administration of the village, district, province, country, and the entire globe is conducted in this manner.”
“What, is there only one nation on the globe?”

“Yes, for a hundred years now. Well then, please permit us, so that we may finish our remaining work. (Glancing at the clock) It is four o’clock; at five we shall depart from here. I will inform the village head of your arrival. In the evening, you must rest there.”
“Yes, you all carry on with your work. I am quite content sitting here.”

As soon as Sumedh awoke, everyone took the path to the garden. Sumedh rang the telephone bell, and the response came immediately. He whispered something, I know not what. Then, after listening for a moment, he said to me, “Our village chief, Devmitra, wishes to speak with you. I must now go to work.” With these words, he too departed for his duties.

I approached the ‘radio-phone.’ There, to my astonishment, I saw the reflection of a man on a glass panel. I gazed in wonder. It was certainly not my own reflection; nor was there any other person present. Yet, it was not a mere picture either. I stood transfixed, bewildered, when suddenly the lips of that image moved and a voice came through the telephone—“Welcome! I am Devmitra. Just now, our friend Sumedh informed me of your auspicious arrival. The most important task at hand is that I am now sending your portrait and news to Patna. From there, within six hours, your image and information will reach the entire globe. When you arrive here, I shall of course be present to welcome you in person, but for now, I do not wish to trouble you further. You must be weary—please rest.”

Though I listened to Devmitra’s words with amazement, I consoled myself that these were all marvels of science. After traveling for so many days, my feet truly felt fatigued, though sleep eluded me. I was just considering lying down when, through the open door into the next room, I noticed a cupboard and, upon the table beside it, some books. My curiosity drew me away from the bed and toward them. Upon closer inspection, I found the cupboard filled with books, all bound in the most exquisite covers. Sitting on a nearby chair, I picked up a book from the table. It felt somewhat heavier than usual. Upon opening it, I discovered its pages were made of some silvery metal. The printing and finish were exceptionally beautiful. I wished to see where it had been printed. Upon examination, I found it was printed at the Nalanda Press in the year 2024. A hundred years had passed since its printing, yet it looked as if it had just come from the press! Opening it, I saw that the pages were exceedingly fine—almost three lines to an inch.

There must have been a thousand pages. At every step, all the events of the present world began to seem astonishing to me. I thought to myself, first I should see which books are here. On the table, to one side, I saw a booklet inscribed in bold letters with an index. Upon inspection, I found that there were two hundred books here related to history, botany, literature, and geography. In terms of language, most of the books were in Hindi. Some were in the universal language, and one or two were in English as well. The book I considered most suitable for the present time was "The History of Universal National Organization." Picking it up, I sat down on a chair. The printing and so forth of the book were unparalleled. It had been published this very year. The author was Vishwamitra, a historian and teacher at Nalanda University. I thought, it would be difficult to read this book of two to two and a half thousand pages in an hour, so I decided to look at the table of contents.

From the table of contents, the major events after 1624 that I learned were these: Under British protection, India attained self-rule by 1640; the United Asian Nation by 1660; the United Asia-Africa-Australia Nation by 2000; the United Europe-America Nation by 2010; and a single nation for the entire globe by 2024. I said to myself, let me see who is the President of the whole world nowadays. For this, I turned to the final chapter of the book, in which, along with the names, there were portraits of those individuals, their birthplaces, and places of education as well. The President of the entire globe, elected for the next three years, is Mr. Dutt, whose birthplace is in India itself. He received his education at Takshashila. His age is seventy-four years. The Prime Minister, Ohdara, is Japanese. The Minister of Education, Monolin, is a Russian woman; the Minister of Health, David, is an American; similarly, the ministers of other departments are people from various countries. I looked very carefully, yet nowhere did I see a Minister of War. It occurred to me, perhaps the name was omitted by a printing error. How could such an important position remain vacant? Later, I looked into the national assemblies of various countries and saw that everywhere there was an absence of a Minister of War. I turned to the index at the end, where the words army, commander-in-chief, and Minister of War appeared...

From reading those pages, it became clear that in the year 2024 A.D., this important institution of the ancient world was abolished. Now, there is neither any army anywhere, nor any commander-in-chief.
I had only just discovered this much when, in the meantime, everyone returned from their work. As soon as they arrived, Sumedh asked me to come along. I stood up.
When we left the house, I saw that everyone simply closed the door behind them and set off. Observing this, I asked—
“Will no one stay here?”
“What for?”
“To look after things; if nothing else, shouldn’t you at least lock the door before leaving?”

“They use locks in the electric factories, out of fear that some stranger might accidentally touch a machine part. Here, who would die from touching books? The doors are closed simply to prevent any animal from getting in and damaging something.”
At the mention of animals, I suddenly remembered that there used to be many monkeys here before; I asked—
“Well, it’s clear now that there’s no possibility of theft. But tell me, I used to see a lot of monkeys around here before—what happened to them? Not a single one is to be seen now.”

“You’re asking about something from more than a hundred years ago. I’ve read in books that, in places where there used to be many monkeys, the government, seeing the damage to crops, made great efforts to catch them. The female monkeys were kept in houses with thousands of cages, and the male monkeys were left on an island. In this way, within twenty to twenty-five years, all the monkeys died out on their own, because their reproduction was halted.”
“So, are there no monkeys left at all?”
“There are a few, kept in large museums for the study of zoology, where their numbers are increased as needed. Monkeys—”
Not only that, there are many other such creatures who now merely add to the splendor of museums, whom people once used to keep with great fondness."
Recalling, I asked, "But dogs and cats—are they still in the villages?"
"No, what benefit do they bring to the village? Their species too can now only be found in museums."
Motors appeared lined up on the road; as we conversed, we each took our respective seats. Each motor had an open space for the Bose-Bon mourners to sit. I asked, "Where did the harvested fruits go?"

"They are plucked at that very moment and loaded onto the motors. It seems that by the time you arrived, the motors had already departed with their loads. If the fruits are kept here for long to dry, they are spoiled, so as soon as they reach the station, they are placed in ice-cooled wagons and sent off to the places where they are needed."
"So, in your village, only fruits are produced?"

"Yes, only fruits; and among them, apple orchards are the most abundant. That is why our village has come to be known as the Apple Village. Fifteen miles from here is Orange Village, where there are only orange groves. You must have seen the banana forest across the Bagmati you asked about."
"Yes, I did see it."
"That lies within the bounds of Banana Village. There, almost only bananas are produced. In our village, there is a small orange grove as well. The banana you ate at breakfast was from there."
"I found a special kind of flavor and sweetness in all the fruits. Their appearance too was remarkable—does that have some reason?"
"Yes, now botany has advanced far beyond your time. To create unique forms, flavors, scents, and shapes in fruits is now in human hands."
Our conversation continued. The motors sped ahead with a whirring sound. On both sides of the road, there were apple orchards lining the way. Though our road...

Here and there, the road would rise or fall by ten or twenty cubits, but the ascent and descent were so gradual that one hardly noticed them. To the right flowed the Bagmati, and to the left stood the mountains. At some places, the Bagmati was four hundred yards below, at others, less than that; yet the gardens stretched all the way to the riverbank. The land had been leveled uniformly. The rocks that once made the ground rugged and uneven had either been covered or broken up and thrown into the river. Witnessing this power of man, I felt both astonishment and delight.

As I pondered, a thought crossed my mind—surely, the crop of Setra oranges does not last all year. What do these people do during the other seasons? Before I could receive an answer, I noticed small fruits hanging in the nearby orchards. I asked, “Are these another variety of apples, so small in size?”

“There is certainly a difference in variety, but not in size. These will grow even larger and redder than the others; their harvest will be ready in two months. Here, the crops are always ripening and being gathered.”
As we spoke, motor cars crossed the railway road. I asked, “Where does this railway go?”
“It passes through Chandragadhi, then to Kathmandu, and from there extends much farther beyond.”

I asked in amazement, “Has the railway reached these mountains? In my time, I saw arrangements for a ‘rope-line’ at Chandragadhi to carry loads. Back then, electric poles were installed from the Phaping power plant for that purpose.”

“There is no such power plant in Phaping now. I have read that once, in Nepal, there was a king named Chandra Shamsher. To benefit his country, he had a power plant built there, but it was shut down over a hundred and fifty years ago.”
“Do you know why it was closed?”
“The water from the mountain streams nearby was collected in a reservoir to generate electricity. Although some electricity was produced from it—”

—was considered sufficient for the expenses of that time, perhaps. But by employing the water from the springs in such a manner, the mountains around Farpig began to dry up. Even if the Moon had undertaken both these tasks with the best of intentions—”
“What was the second task?”
“The second task was to have the mountains and the surrounding forests cleared and turned into fields.”
“What harm was there in that?”
“That too caused the mountains to gradually dry up—rainfall began to decrease. In the end, within just fifty years, due to the lack of water, people had to abandon those fields and flee.”
“So, did shutting down that factory bring any benefit?”

“Yes, a great deal. If you go there now, you’ll find the mountains around Farpig lush and green with delightful gardens. All around, you’ll see orchards of apples, pears, grapes, and pomegranates flourishing. All these fruits grow there, and they are very large and sweet. In this way, with the forests of gardens taking root, the profit now is many times greater than before. The mountains have become moist again; there are many springs, too.”
“Then, a great revolution must have taken place everywhere! Well, now perhaps your village is near as well. Are those the houses I see?”
“Yes, those are the ones; but it’s still three miles away—just a ten-minute walk.”
“Have you ever traveled in Nepal?”

“Yes, very much. My annual vacations have often been spent traveling there and in Tibet. I have lived here for thirty years. Every year, I get a two-month vacation. I have spent ten or twelve holidays traveling there. From both a geographical and economic perspective, I have studied those places in great detail.”

Hearing such things from this man, my astonishment only grew. In the twentieth century, such a man would have been a professor at some fine college. But today, he is among the common people. Has the value of knowledge diminished, or—
Has the esteem for scholarship risen? I asked, “Does your knowledge benefit others as well?”

“Why not? We are only required to perform our duty for three hours. What else is there to do with the rest of the time? I have often delivered lectures here on my specialized subjects, and during holidays, I have gone to other provinces and countries to lecture as well. I also contribute discussions to monthly journals.”
“Well, that is good; but tell me, what things does Nepal produce?”

“In terms of minerals, we have copper, iron, and lead here. Coal used to be mined for our needs, but now, with the increased use of electricity, coal is not as necessary. Electricity from here is supplied to Videha, Malla, and Kosala, and this electricity is generated from the waterfalls of several rivers. Even this train is run by that electricity. Our automobiles are powered by it as well. Besides this, Nepal is a treasure trove of fruits and nuts. There are millions of sheep and many blanket factories here. Nepal supplies more than half of India with warm clothing.”
“So it appears that rice and wheat are not grown here.”

“No; these things come from other provinces. Nowadays, whatever can be best produced in a place is grown there. Generally, a village produces only one thing. Other necessary items are brought in from elsewhere.”
We were approaching the first house of the village. I saw the same man whose image I had seen in the telephone, standing with a few others to welcome me. I was received with hospitality.

I noticed that all the men and women were beautiful and clean. Along the roadside were rows of handsome houses. All the houses were alike and without upper stories. It all seemed to me a completely new world. I was still pondering these things when Devmitra said to me, “This way.”

I fell behind. All those men and women were with me. It was now half past five. The house toward which we were heading bore, in bold letters, the inscription—‘Guest Rest House.’ As soon as we arrived, the village head gentleman asked a man standing there, “Comrade Dev! Which room has been prepared for today’s guest to rest in?”
Dev replied, “Why, the fifth room right here.”

We had just reached the door of the room when, from the adjacent room, another gentleman emerged, whose age must have been between seventy and eighty. He too welcomed us. Now we entered the room. The village head said:

“At this time, we will not trouble you further. You are weary from your journey. Please rest for a while. At eight o’clock, after dinner, all the villagers eager to meet you will gather in the assembly hall. You already know me. These days, I am the village head (president of the village council) here. These other twenty men and women are members of the village council. This other guest is Vishwamitra, a professor of history at Nalanda University. He had gone to Tibet for some historical research and has just arrived here by airship today. Afterward, you will have the opportunity to converse with him and learn more. This is Comrade Dev.”

After a short while, the others took their leave of me and departed. Dev quickly turned on the electric light, for the sun had now set. The mountain chill was gently seeping in. Although Sumedh had given me a woolen cloak on the way, it was not quite enough. Dev turned on the heater, and soon the room grew warm. I sat on a chair and invited Vishwamitra to sit as well, if he had no urgent business. He took the other chair.
From the name of the author on the historical treatise I had seen in the garden, I was fairly certain that this was indeed the same Vishwamitra; yet, I...

He asked, “Are you Professor Vishwamitra, the author of ‘The History of the Organization of the Universal Nation’?” He replied with humility, “Yes, that is I.” “Then I am very pleased to meet you.” “Even more so, our Nalanda family always remembers you. You will be pleased to see the seed you once sowed there. It was only after your conversation with Gramani Mahashay that I learned of your auspicious arrival. The entire school community there is very eager. Our Acharya Vashishtha just told me that the Nalanda family has the first right to see you.” “Did you learn all this through the telephone?” “Yes. In fact, I was just speaking on the telephone in the library. I have already informed them of your arrival here. They have said, if it is not inconvenient, to request you for a conversation and a meeting at this very moment.” “No, not at all. It is no inconvenience to me. After all, I have come on foot! Let us go, then. It is no less a pleasure for me as well.” Saying this, we both rose and went to the library. Here was an open hall, large enough to seat a hundred to a hundred and fifty people. There were two bookcases filled with books. Electric lights were shining. In the center stood large tables, and many chairs were arranged for sitting. Vishwamitra went and rang the telephone bell. I sat down on a chair nearby. After a few moments, he said to me, “Our Acharya is waiting for you.” I went and saw, in the glass, the reflection of an elderly man. The reflection moved its lips, bowed its head, and from the telephone came the voice, “Welcome.” I too bowed my head in response. Vishwamitra said, “This is our Acharya. He has served the school for seventy years, of which he has held the position of Acharya for the last twenty.” I said, “Vashishthaji, I am truly delighted to meet you.”
"Truly, you are all blessed, who, through such ceaseless imparting of knowledge, are serving the world."
"It is our duty... Yes, on behalf of the Nalanda family, I have a request: before accepting any invitation elsewhere, please visit our institution first."
"That is my own wish as well; nothing more need be said about it. From here, I shall come directly there."

"It is also a matter of joy that Teacher Vishwamitra is at your service. He is now returning to the institution; please accompany him. Your body is exceedingly frail. Therefore, we do not insist that you come immediately."
"Certainly, I am coming there directly from here. Convey my good wishes to all the boys and girls, and to the entire family of teachers."
"Everyone is listening here through the word-broadcaster. Well then, please take rest now."
This conversation filled my heart with a wondrous joy. Holding Vishwamitra's hand, I returned from there to my room. I said—

"Vishwamitra! There is a great difference between the world of my time and the world now. You are a teacher of history—you know these things. But it seems all the more astonishing to me, for I have seen with these very eyes the world as it was two hundred years ago. Those events seem as if they happened only yesterday. At that time, there was but a faint whisper of equality; yet, who could have imagined such a form, even in dreams? Today itself, I have arrived in your world. As yet, I have not seen or understood even a hundredth part of it. Still, in this much alone, I am drowning in a sea of wonder. It brings me joy to see that your world has progressed beyond all hope."

chapters.title: About the School
paragraphs: “Well then, tell me this—what is the present state of the Nalanda University?”

“Nalanda is now a vast institution. From the old Bargaon all the way to Rajgriha, the buildings and hostels of the university stretch unbroken. Nowhere else in the world is there another institution like it for the study of philosophy and history. Students come here to study from Europe, America, Japan, Africa, Australia—from every corner of the globe. The world’s largest museum of ancient artifacts is here. The arrangements for teaching and learning ancient scripts and languages are the finest to be found anywhere.

By the order of the ‘Universal Union’, not only is material related to the history of India collected here, but also countless resources concerning Rome, Greece, Egypt, Assyria, Chaldea, Mexico, and many others. Nalanda takes pride in having greatly aided the presentation of international history. The study of philosophy at Nalanda is conducted in the most excellent manner. There are provisions for the study of all philosophies—modern, ancient, Eastern, and Western. Our professors are great scholars of philosophy. There are teachers here for Sanskrit, Pali, Zend, Prakrit, Greek, Latin (Roman), and many other languages.

A true revolution has taken place in the study of languages. For each language, an appropriate environment for study has been created. Students with a special interest in particular languages are kept here in such a way that their connection with other languages is almost entirely severed. All their conversations take place in that language alone. The names of objects and so forth are explained by the teachers through demonstrations, all in the target language. In this way, within three years, the students gain mastery over the language.

The study of astronomy, too, is best conducted at Nalanda in all of India. On the Vaibhara Hill of Rajgriha stands the university’s great observatory. Our institution has contributed to the growth of astronomical literature as well. The universities of ‘Nalanda’ and ‘Takshashila’ in India are among the foremost seats of learning in the world.”
"Takshashila has earned great renown in the sciences of Ayurveda, botany, zoology, and others."
"What is the duration of study in the school? What are the rules and the examination system like?"

"Seventeen years of study are compulsory for everyone. This rule is the same not only for India but for all the schools across the globe. In the third year, a child is admitted to the kindergarten. After that, for six years, he attends the infant class; from six to fourteen, the children's class; and from fourteen to twenty, the youth class. Generally, education ends here. After this, boys take up different professions according to their inclinations and abilities. However, those whose inclination is found to be towards scholarship are given further opportunities to enhance their expertise in their chosen field. This period usually lasts from four to six years. But there is no fixed duration for this. Even after this, those who continue their studies have full opportunity to advance further.

In this way, our conversation continued on many subjects. We were still talking when it was almost eight o'clock. Meanwhile, the gracious Padmavati of the guest house had come and greeted us, but seeing our serious discussion, she thought it best not to interrupt and quietly left. Now she returned to inform us that it was nearly eight o'clock and the meal gong was about to sound. We should get ready to go.
I asked Vishwamitra, "Why is this gong sounded?"

"The thing is, the nation did not consider it appropriate for everyone to waste money on keeping a watch. That is why time is announced in this manner. There are four times for refreshments and meals in the day and night—at seven in the morning, breakfast; at eleven, midday meal; at three or three-thirty, tea; and..."
Then, at eight o’clock in the evening, supper. At these four times, as well as at the time of waking in the morning, a cannon is fired.”
“But, I saw a watch with Sumedhji in the garden?”
“Yes, among those who go out to work, the chief person carries a watch—not everyone. Well then, now we must be going. Here, take this—the cannon too— Ararar—Dham!”

We set out from there quickly. Dev, Padmavati, and the two of us—four people in all. All around us on the road, the electric lights spread like moonlight. The road was broad and clean. On both sides stood rows of solid, uniform houses. In front of each house, flower plants stretched up to the road, their beauty and fragrance delighting the hearts of passersby. Before every house was a veranda, shared by a hundred houses together.

Vishwamitraji explained that each person has three rooms to live in. The front room, the drawing room, is as large as the one we have just come from. Ten chairs could easily be arranged there. Behind it, in width one and a half times as large, but half as long, are two rooms—one for sleeping, the other for bathing. These three rooms together make up a house. A hundred such houses form a single row. Each row has an elected head, who also lives in one of the houses of that row. I later learned that Sumedh is the head of such a row. Each row has a spacious hall, where there are some books, musical instruments, and other items for entertainment. Here too, a telephone is installed. There are twenty-five such rows in this Apple Village.

Men and women walked along the road, conversing with one another. The subject of all their talk seemed to be me. I saw thousands of men and women on the way, but not a single child among them. I understood then—after three years, the children are taken away. Perhaps, due to the cold, they do not bring small children out at this hour. Now, on a large nearby building, I saw, in bold letters...

chapters.title: The Twentieth Century
paragraphs: I saw the ‘dining hall’. An extraordinary brilliance of electric light was scattered all around. There were many doors to enter the building. Before entering, people washed their hands at the hot water taps in the veranda and dried them with the hanging towels. Then they went inside. The tables and chairs for serving food were just like those I had seen in the garden. The hall was very long and wide. Five thousand people could easily sit and dine there in comfort. The cleanliness and interior beauty were unparalleled. The kitchen, it seemed, was separate and to the back. As soon as I arrived, the villagers and other previously acquainted men and women also gathered there. I was seated on a chair. On my right was Devamitra, and on my left, Vishwamitra. The food had already been served and was ready. Among the dishes were bread, meat, and two kinds of vegetables. There was also a bowl of halwa, a small plate of fruit, and a glass of water.

We had to sit for two minutes after arriving, then a bell rang out, upon which Devamitra said, “Now the meal should begin.” This waiting is done so that all those who are to eat may arrive. That dining assembly seemed very strange to me. Here and there, women sat among the men, eating without any hesitation. I said to myself, “When could Indians of the twentieth century ever dream of such a thing?” Although I had not yet asked, and by their appearance, education, civility, and purity, all the men and women seemed to be of a high caste, still I wondered in my mind, “Are all these Brahmins or Kshatriyas?” I had already heard something—Arjan’s parents were residents of Lanka. Though everyone’s dress and attire were the same, many men and women appeared as fair as Europeans.
From all these things, it became certain in my mind that “all this is but one caste.”

After finishing their meal, everyone rose and exited through their respective doors, washed their hands at the hot water taps, and after wiping their faces, left the place. The Gramani had already said that there would be a gathering in the assembly hall. So, we set out for there. Yes, I also noticed that although everyone washed their hands and faces...
However, no one removed their shoes to wash their feet, nor did anyone take off their other clothes.
Now we proceeded from there to the Assembly Hall; this magnificent building was only a little distance away.

The structure was very tall and beautiful—outside, electric lights glittered brilliantly. Here too, in bold illuminated letters above the main entrance, was written ‘Assembly Hall’. We entered inside.

Devmitra said, “Until everyone arrives, please sit in the room behind the stage.” We had scarcely sat there for a short while when suddenly the sound of a bell rang from the stage, upon hearing which the village chief signaled us to proceed. As soon as I entered, all eyes turned toward me. The internal splendor of the ‘Assembly Hall’ was utterly enchanting.

On the stage, various colorful and strange paintings shone under the bright electric lamps. The ceiling of the building was very high. Large windows were set in the walls. The electric garlands made night as bright as day. Although it was cold outside, the windows and doors were open on all sides, yet, thanks to the concealed heating devices, no trace of chill could be felt within. The walls and ceilings were adorned with beautiful, multicolored vines and motifs. Here and there, large portraits of great men hung—thinkers, poets, and all kinds of illustrious figures. Somewhere was Buddha, elsewhere Rousseau, here Marx, there Engels; Socrates, Plato, Lenin, Newton, and many other world-renowned personalities graced that spacious hall. In between, many wise sayings were displayed.

I looked toward the gathering; there was no one thin or pale. Men and women alike sat upon cushioned benches. In that vast hall, there must have been five thousand people seated, yet even the benches at the back could easily accommodate more. This building served all political and literary purposes. The meetings of the village council were held here. For entertainment, distinguished guests from outside or local experts delighted everyone here with music and dramatic performances.
are held here. Lectures by scholars on history, science, and other subjects also take place here. Many national and social festivals are celebrated in this place.

As soon as everyone had quietly taken their seats, Devmitra rose and proposed the name of Mr. Ismail to preside over today’s assembly. While making the proposal, he said, “Although comrade Ismail is well-known to all of us at heart, for the information of our esteemed guest today, it seems necessary to mention that comrade Ismail has, on many occasions, served as the head of our village and as the president of the Nepal Republic. Though he is only sixty years old, by virtue we all consider him venerable. There is another matter that brings him even closer to our guest today. Not only is he a son of the Nalanda school, but our guest will surely recall the name of the great man Shafi; you are the grandson of that illustrious Vaishali-born sage. You are counted among the world’s foremost political experts. Our province, and especially our Apple Village, take pride in you, where you have resided ever since completing your education.”

The proposal was accepted with a round of applause, and Ismail stood up. Truly, the radiance of a great soul shone upon his face at a mere glance. In fact, he should be called a sixty-year-old youth. Not only he, but men of sixty or seventy years in this era appear as robust and vigorous as men of thirty-five or forty in the twentieth century. Just as the world has progressed in other matters, so too in this. Mr. Ismail said—

“Comrades! The only reason for me to be accepted for this service in the presence of so many wise and venerable people can be nothing but your unmerited kindness. I was simply lost in joy upon receiving the message of the arrival of such a great soul. I am proud that I have not only been born into Nalanda through learning, but my birth itself is from there. My grandfather, as you all know, lived to the full age of one hundred and fifty years. He used to tell us how, in what hardships, Nalanda’s...”

He was revived. When he was twenty-five years old, he dedicated his life to the school, and in the end, it was there that he entered the fire and attained samadhi. He used to say that, along with him, many great men served Nalanda at that time. In those days, small villages were scattered at intervals across the land of the school. The ruins of the ancient buildings of the institution stood like mounds. Back then, the Budh-Pokhar and similar places did not possess their present beauty. There was a small village named Badgaon, where even now stands a temple of the Sun. The fair of Kartik’s Surya-Shashthi lasted only a single day, and it was mostly women who participated in it. You know, at that time, the reign of selfishness prevailed. Men considered the education of women a threat to religion. Our Muslim brothers, in the name of religion, had bound women in chains, and following their example, all of northern India had become a solitary prison for womankind. Consider it a great mercy that women were even able to attend that fair in the name of religion.

Everyone had heard that Acharya Vishwabandhu, after serving the school for thirty years, had gone to Uttarakhand, and since then, nothing was known of him. But who could have hoped that such fortune would dawn upon us? Three generations have waited. Whenever we heard these stories, we dreamed—if only we could see that great man again, if only he would return, we would carry him upon our heads and eyes. We have never witnessed such atrocities against women since birth. We have never even heard the words of caste or hierarchy among men. We have not even heard tales of people killing and dying in the name of religion. But you have read in history—here stands Vishwamitra, the teacher who brought honor to your country. Now, when we read in the histories about massacres committed in the name of religion, we laugh—just as we laugh at tales of thousands of men burning like moths in the fires of war at the whim of a king. Blessed are those who, in that age of darkness, strove with the effort of Bhagirath for the welfare of humanity.
Today, the sacred image of the great man Vishwabandhu is among us. (Pointing towards the portraits of the great men) Today, we understand that all these gods—
Suppose, the living one is among us. Truly, can the feelings of our hearts, our outpourings of devotion, ever be expressed through words?

“Comrades! The greatest fortune of our village is that you have come here first. Today, indeed, an indescribable ocean of joy is surging within our hearts. How should we worship this venerable soul, how should we welcome him, we do not know. What offering do we possess that is worthy of such an extraordinary great man? Not much, only this—O Mahatma! We are all grateful to you; we can never repay our debt to you. Comrades, though we all yearn to hear something from your lips, yet such a desire would be an imposition upon you. A body of two hundred and sixty years, and within it, a long fast of two hundred years. So be it. Now, what more can I say on behalf of all of us in service to the Mahatma, except this: O noble soul! We are grateful to you, and we can never be worthy of being free from your debt.”
I listened to all these words with great attentiveness. As I listened, countless scenes from the past flitted before my mind’s eye. When the speech ended, I stood up and said—

“Brothers! What I am seeing now was once only a dream, for the realization of which millions offered up their lives and all they possessed. You can imagine what joy fills my heart to see that dream living and breathing before my very eyes. Even now, how much of today’s world have I truly seen? Yet, what I have seen—is that not enough? Suppose, today I were to go to some village of 1623, would I find a village like this Seb-gram? Your village, with its population of five thousand—let me tell you the condition of such villages in those days. Mud huts, in which the very earth of the walls has crumbled in places. Somewhere a corner has collapsed. Thatched roofs and broken tiles lie scattered. Out of ten houses, perhaps two are such that the rain does not drip inside. In narrow alleys everywhere, heaps of refuse are thrown, and there the foul water of the drains flows. Children sit right there to relieve themselves.

During the rainy season, the filth and stench would become even more overwhelming. The fields surrounding the settlement served as the only places for people to relieve themselves. Dogs roamed everywhere. Somehow, with great difficulty, the only path where a cart could pass was considered the road of that time. Where are those bullock carts and ekkas now? You must have seen them in museums of ancient artifacts. Those were the vehicles of that era. Wealthy people kept fine horse-drawn carriages. Elephants, too, were kept for riding. But now, here among you, it is only the motorcar for travel, only the motorcar for transport—every village task is accomplished by motor vehicles. In those days, all these tasks were done by men or bullock carts. I myself, on several occasions, traveled eight or ten kos through the night, riding atop a bullock cart.

“Yes, I was describing that village. In the middle, on either side of the narrow village road, there were shops: the sweet-sellers sold batashas and laddus, the cloth merchants sold fabrics, the grocers sold spices and colors; some sold vegetables, some needles and thread, some salt and oil. Once or twice a week, large markets were held, when more people would come from the neighboring villages to buy their necessities. Some bought goods with money, others bartered with grain. The shopkeepers made their living from this buying and selling. What can I say about the condition of the people? If you were to see even the wealthiest man of that time, you would call him a god. Boys of five or six years would run about wearing only a four-finger-wide strip of cloth for a loincloth. Except for a few wealthy people, generally everyone managed with just a towel and a dhoti. Even those were dirty and tattered, and many had nothing but rags. The women, too, made do with a single soiled sari, which they continued to wear even after it was reduced to tatters, patching it again and again. I saw many such women in Bundelkhand, whose skirts were so worn out that, except for the seams at the folds, there was hardly a finger’s width of intact cloth left; otherwise, one could see right through them. What could they do? Such was their poverty.”

“Then what oppression was there? For women to wear shoes was, among many castes at that time, considered a sin; and even if it were not, where would they have the fortune to obtain them? In the winter months, if someone managed to sew together rags and tatters into a single patched quilt, know that they had attained great prosperity. Laying straw on the ground, the children and all would huddle together beneath that quilt to sleep. Not everyone was fortunate enough to have a cot to sleep on. Due to the scarcity of clothing, many had to spend the winter covered only with straw. Where was the luck to have firewood to warm themselves? If they managed to gather some grass or dry leaves, the family would sit contentedly by its side, inhaling a little smoke for a while.

“I remember it well. Once, in the winter, I was walking along a road very early in the morning. On that same road, an old woman was coming, dressed in a torn, dirty, and tattered sari, carrying something in a winnowing basket. Behind her followed two boys, four or five years old. The elder had a loincloth; the younger did not have a single thread on his body. It was the bitter cold of the months of Magh and Paush. Both children were shivering from the cold. They had clenched their fists tightly and bent their waists against the chill. Such boys were not one or two, but millions in India at that time.

“Even rotten, spoiled grain was not available in sufficient quantity for millions to fill their stomachs. Many people wandered from village to village begging for food. With my own eyes I saw, in many places, boys and men snatching discarded scraps from the mouths of dogs to eat. It was not that people shied away from hard work. There may have been a few like that, but most were such that, from four in the morning until eight, even ten at night, they toiled hungry and thirsty in fields, shops, and factories—yet even then, they could not obtain enough coarse, rough cloth for their bodies or enough food to fill their bellies. If they fell ill, their troubles only increased. On one side, the blow of disease; on the other, the lack of medicine and doctors; and on top of that, nowhere any certainty of food.
“It was December of 1918, when, in just four or five weeks, sixty lakh (six million) people died in India from a single illness—influenza.”

Most of those who died were poor, who had neither clothes to protect themselves from the cold, nor food for nourishment, nor money for medicine, nor a clean house to live in. That was not an animal’s life, but a life of hell. People died like dogs and cats. I am not familiar with the language and definitions of the present day, so I am speaking in that old tongue itself. It is possible that you may, at times, find it difficult to understand.

“Ladies and gentlemen! At the time when the majority of the country’s people were living such lives, there were very few who were in somewhat better circumstances; these were, in the language of that age, called the ‘well-to-do.’ Yes, there was also a group, countable on one’s fingers, for whom every kind of pleasure was easily available. These were the wealthy, known by names such as nawab, king, babu, taluqdar, great landlords, seth-sahukar, mahajan, and factory owners. Although, among them, there were one or two rare individuals who were moved by the suffering of the aforementioned wretches, their number was negligible.

The rich lived in grand palaces—two-storied, four-storied, even five-storied mansions. For the service of their bodies alone, they required a great many male and female attendants. Some kings had two or three hundred maidservants; their harems were filled with two or four hundred women. Even so, these people were called the stalwarts of religion. To ruin someone’s honor, to seize another’s property—these were deeds accomplished at their mere gesture. When they walked, hundreds of people went before and behind them for their protection. Some traveled in palanquins, carried by men! Abuse was ever an ornament upon their lips. At the slightest provocation, they would thus ‘honor’ their own people. While they slept, others pressed their feet, fanned them. They considered it beneath their dignity to do any work with their own hands. For one man, there would be many motorcars, horse-drawn carriages, carts, riding horses, and elephants. Many of them spent their days and nights intoxicated with liquor, bhang, or opium. They themselves did not labor at all.

They were experts at setting fire to the earnings of others’ hard labor. There were few who would soothe another’s wounds, but many who would rub salt into them. The amount these people spent on food and clothing for a single body of their own could have allowed a thousand people to live happily. For their solitary comfort, they possessed houses big enough to accommodate hundreds. The most intolerable thing was that, despite being the very embodiment of vice and oppression, these people wished to assume the form of religion and occupy an unshakable place in the world; and if some of them ever succeeded in this, it is hardly doubtful. They did not understand the value of humanity before them. Their spell was cast over judges, religious leaders, scholars, Maulvis, and priests alike. All of them echoed their words, ever ready to cite proofs from their own scriptures for the benefit of these people.

The scholars would say, “The rich and the poor, the king and the subject, are all the result of deeds from previous births. This has been so since time immemorial. Such is the will of God. The Vedas and Puranas all bear witness to this.” The Maulvis would say, “God created the rich and the poor, the king and the commoner, for the welfare of the world; otherwise, how would the world function? All the Prophets and Messengers accepted this and were content with their fate. The king and the master are under God’s shadow.” Thus did all sing in the same tune. The truth was that, after snatching away the share of millions of laborers, the rich did not consume everything themselves; they tossed a few crumbs to these people as well, and the latter considered it their duty to echo their benefactors’ words.
Thanks be that now, that spell has been broken.

“Now, hearing all this, it must astonish you— Were those millions truly sheep, to be made to dance at the flick of a rich man’s finger? If only people had used their own intelligence, why would they have remained in bondage? Truly, today this reasoning seems simple, but at that time, such thoughts seemed impossible—like the castles in the air of Sheikh Chilli. Anyone who even entertained a fraction of the ideas we now hold would have been considered mad, eccentric, irreligious, an enemy of humanity. After receiving an education, every man...

Everyone wanted to become part of that wealthy class, though perhaps only one in a thousand ever succeeded. In this way, the educated and the rich paid no attention to this principle, and the poor considered it impossible. They were so ensnared by their own feeble notions that, truly, such a thing seemed utterly unattainable to them. You may say—what foolishness is this? What could be so difficult about understanding that, instead of letting others eat the fruits of our own hard labor, we ourselves should partake of them? Yet, for them, this was like chewing iron grains. On the other hand, the wealthy would say—if this were to happen, religion would perish; caste honor would be lost, the age of darkness would descend.

Unfortunately, even the laboring people were divided into numerous higher and lower castes. The Brahmin laborer of Bihar would say—so what if we are poor, so what if we have nothing to eat, but at least the Chamars, Ahirs, and Rajputs bow to us and address us as ‘Maharaj’. How could it be that Chamars and Ahirs become our equals? Truly, that would be a great sin! Better to die of hunger; better that another eats the fruit of our toil; but to consider a Chamar as equal to ourselves—not at all. Similarly, the pride of the higher-caste Pathans and Sayyids—though the Momins and weavers of Mawn might not truly consider them superior in their hearts—would not wish to allow the sweepers, whom they counted as beneath themselves, to become their equals.

“Now, finally, let me say a few words about your present goal, and then I shall conclude my address. First and foremost, do not think that we have reached the final destination; that all our aims have been fulfilled, that there is no flaw left within us. The moment such a thought arises, from that very moment you will begin to slide backward—your decline will commence. How far humanity can progress is boundless. Just as, some time ago, a very distant star was discovered in astronomy, and then another even farther was found; in the same way, for millions of years, ever more distant stars will be revealed through telescopes and photographic images. In this way, our progress, the field of our research, stretches infinitely far. The second point is the growth of knowledge. There is no doubt that the pinnacle of education in those days is now but the beginning of its ascent.

Your society is highly educated and civilized; yet, by advancing, you can turn today’s end into tomorrow’s beginning. Your successors also possess this right. It is a matter of great joy that today, knowledge can be pursued for the benefit of all humanity. Today, knowledge is not awarded the same prizes or value as it was two centuries ago. The root of all present prosperity is that very knowledge—that very learning—which, in its absence, once caused people to fall from their humanity. Neglect in its growth and carelessness in its dissemination are the root of all evils. The desire for progress and the widest possible spread of knowledge—these are the two fundamental principles by which you have advanced so far, and before you still lies an infinite field for further progress. I am deeply satisfied by your affectionate sentiments. And that is all.”

At the conclusion of my lecture, my companion Ismail once again rose to thank me, and the assembly was dismissed. I, along with Vishwamitra, Ismail, Devamitra, Ismail’s wife Priyamvada, and other gentlemen, proceeded to the resting place. It was already ten o’clock at night. In response to their inquiries and requests, I briefly said, “Tomorrow, the day after, and on the third day, I shall remain here to study the surroundings and your village. After that, I will go directly to Nalanda with Teacher Vishwamitra. From there, after studying the conditions of the principal places of India, I shall set foot elsewhere. Please inform the Sovereign Union President, Mr. Dutt, of this as well.”

Devamitra said, “Companion Ismail and Sister Priyamvada will also remain with you, and will assist you in understanding matters here.” I expressed my gratitude for this. After that, everyone departed for their respective places. At the time of parting, Ismail too did not offer a formal greeting. I had already noticed a glimpse of these people’s detachment from religion, and had felt a desire to inquire about it. Now that desire grew even stronger. Vishwamitra was sitting nearby. I asked—
“Vishwamitra! Although I have heard people’s names such as Hindu and Muslim, yet—”
“There is no difference in their dress, conversation, or greetings—have all religions merged together?”
“They have not merged; we have cast out these religions, which were obstacles to progress. There have been many changes in names as well, yet people choose whatever names they wish.”

“And language? At present, the mother tongue of all India is ‘Bharati’, which you may call the representative of the Hindi-Urdu of your time. This is the only language spoken everywhere, and the script is Nagari. Now there are no difficulties of language. In different provinces, other languages are studied out of literary or religious curiosity; but ‘Bharati’ is the supreme language. No matter which province an Indian belongs to, his language will be Bharati. Now that the old prejudices are gone, everyone’s language, sentiments, and attire have become one.”

I did not think it proper to delay any longer. From the orderliness of the time, I had already surmised that there must be some rule regarding sleep as well. Vishwamitra, too, retired to his room to sleep. I also went to the bed in the room where I had slept before and lay down. Sleep had not yet come to my eyes. On the wall before me, an electric, trunk-shaped lamp was spreading its light. The heater was warming the house, and there was no trace of cold. It seemed to be the fifteenth night. The moon had begun to peer into my room from above the treetops. The mountain in front was some distance away. Moonlight was scattered all around. The night was still. As soon as I lay down on my bed, the rumble of a train reached my ears. In the silence of the night, one by one, each scene from today began to replay itself in my mind. Along with this, I began to make my own independent comments on each.

As the scene of women’s freedom appeared before me, I thought—so now, what is the need for those veils drawn over every hand, and the sack-like burqas? Where now will you find women counting two twenties, four twenties? Now, when children ask, mothers who used to tell strange tales about the spots on the moon, the stars, the Milky Way...

Where will they be found? At the thought of the wealthy, it occurred to me—now, surely, no one would die to become a Rajabahadur, Maharajabahadur, Raybahadur, Khanbahadur, or Nawabbahadur. The givers and recipients of these titles have bid farewell to the earth forever. As the scene of today’s village appeared before me, the image of the old village began to fade from my heart. Perhaps it was for this very reason—that its knowledge should not come so easily. I said to myself—what does it matter if you do not show it? You cannot prevent me from seeing it in the museum of wonders.

One by one, all the notes were finished. Meanwhile, the clock struck eleven. I said, soon it will be twelve as well; it is better to think a little about tomorrow’s duties and then go to sleep. I thought—I have seen and heard enough about the orchards of Seb-gram. I have also learned about the houses and their classes. I have seen the community halls and dining halls too. Sumedh had said that children are sent to schools as soon as they turn three. I must see how children live until the age of three, and visit the hospital as well; I want to know about the village’s cleanliness and such matters—these are the main things. Both Ismail and Vishwabhitra are men of wide experience. It would be even better to see everything with them. With these thoughts, I surrendered myself to the lap of the goddess of sleep.

I awoke before five o’clock. I rose and, at that hour, gazed out the window at the sky. Stars were scattered all around. The moon was not before me, yet moonlight was visible. In the moonlight, the flowers laden on the vines outside the window could be seen clearly. The gentle fragrance of roses crept softly into my room. Barely ten or fifteen minutes had passed when the sound of the gong was heard. It was five o’clock. In a little while, Dev...

They too arrived. First, they peeked in; when they saw me sitting, they entered. They asked, “Will you bathe now? If so, would you prefer to bathe here at the house tap in the bathing vessel, or in the hot pool of the bathhouse?”

I replied, “I will bathe here.” Yesterday, I had not even felt the urge for defecation. Now, Dev informed me that the latrine was at the back. And that each house had its own separate latrine, fitted with a tap. After using the latrine, turning the tap released a powerful stream of water that washed away the waste through the pipes. Later, I also learned that no sweepers were employed for the latrines. In fact, there was no such caste as sweepers anymore. Yes, if a tap broke, any person appointed for the maintenance of taps would come and fix it. The waste of the entire village was carried through large pipes to a distance of two or three kos. There, great pits, dug by machines, stood ready. The earth below was excavated, and the rest was piled around the sides. On one side, the waste kept falling, and on the other, a machine kept throwing earth over it. The machines ran on electricity, and the operators stayed at a distance. Although, since the waste was covered with earth and did not come into contact with the open air, there was no stench; yet, the operators would go there if the machines broke down. When one pit was filled, another was already prepared in advance. In this way, a filled pit was left sealed for four years. Afterwards, it was dug up, mixed with some chemicals, and then used as fertilizer for trees.

I sprang up from my bed at once. First, I went to relieve myself. The latrine was clean—it did not seem like a latrine at all. I had not yet gone to the back of the house. I saw that, for ten hands’ length from the house, the ground was adorned with the same flowers, vines, and foliage as in the front. The entire row of ‘Guest Rest’ was surrounded before and behind by a park-like garden, which appeared most beautiful. I looked behind and saw that all the rows were managed in the same way. Keeping the gardens in front of their houses neat, and maintaining the cleanliness and purity of their own homes, was each householder’s responsibility. After returning from the latrine, I went to the bathing room. Upon entering...

chapters.title: The Village and the Villagers
paragraphs: I saw that there were two taps, one for cold water and one for hot. Like white milk, a vessel of porcelain—strong as stone—two hands long, one and a half hands wide, and two hands deep: was this bathing vessel not a small pool itself, embedded in the ground! Beside the tap, attached to the wall, was a place for a bar of soap, and above it, on some hooks, hung a white towel and a freshly washed lungi. The hot water tap was open, and the basin was filled to the brim; yet, the water did not overflow. I washed my hands and feet. Then I thought, now I should clean my teeth. But I saw no twig for brushing; however, near the soap, I noticed a silver box with a toothbrush on top. Upon opening the box, I found fragrant tooth powder within. I reflected that it seemed the custom of using twigs for brushing teeth had vanished. Later, Vishwamitra explained that a single Sebagram would require five thousand twigs daily. Here, after all, there are no useless trees. If good trees were to be cut for twigs, every day one or two trees would be ruined for just one village. And then, the population of the globe is one and a half billion. That is why arrangements have been made for brushes and tooth powder. After all, do we let the shells of almonds and such go to waste? From them, tooth powder or some other useful item is made.

I cleaned my teeth and mouth with the brush and powder, then entered the pool and bathed thoroughly, scrubbing myself well with soap. Thus, after bathing and changing my clothes, Dev came in, turned a tap, and all the water from the bathing vessel drained away. In the same room, by a window on one side, a clean mat was spread on a raised platform. I went there and did some exercise. After this, I came into the sitting room. By now, the red glow of the sun had spread across the eastern sky. Only a thin golden line of the sun’s disc was visible. Here and there, the sweet chirping of birds still continued. Gusts of wind were swaying the flowers in front. The beauty and cleanliness of the street and the houses opposite were scattered all around. My mind, too, was utterly calm and content.
Just then, Vishwamitra arrived. Padmavati was with him. At my invitation, both of them sat down on the chairs placed nearby. Although their faces—

Everyone’s entire body was covered; yet, in the warm house, where was the cold? There are thousands of things worth describing. How could one describe them all? The attire of men and women was not only exceedingly beautiful to behold, but there was nothing in it that was useless, superfluous, or harmful. During working hours, I saw both men and women wearing woolen shorts, long stockings underneath, and a kind of shoe that covered the whole foot. To my astonishment, I noticed that there was nothing made of leather there. Even the shoes were made of a kind of thick jean (which appeared to be leather at first glance), with sturdy rubber soles. The dogs wore a warm coat underneath, and everyone had the same kind of cap on their heads. However, it seemed that this was the work attire, for at night, during dinner and in the assembly hall, this dress was not worn. Instead, everyone wore a round cap on their heads, long warm coats reaching to their feet, and trousers underneath.

The women’s dress consisted of shoes, stockings, a sari, and a kurti. When the cold grew harsher, they would also wear a long warm coat and a cap on their heads. Neither men nor women wore any kind of jewelry. There was no custom of wristwatches or pocket watches either. Those with weak eyesight, who needed them, wore spectacles. I saw that each person had a fountain pen and a diary. When I wished to write the events of the previous day, I too was given a large diary and a fountain pen. The nib was almost entirely of gold, though perhaps, for the sake of durability, a bit of iridium was affixed to the tip. The clip was also of gold. The fact is, what other use is there for gold now? Pounds and coins are no longer in circulation. People do not wear ornaments, nor is there any use for hoarding it. Therefore, it is used in such things as these.

Shortly after Vishwamitra and Padmavati arrived, Ismail also came with his companion Priyamvada and said, “It is nearly seven o’clock. After breakfast today, it would be good to visit the ‘Children’s Garden.’ Priyamvada is the assistant superintendent there. At present, the chief superintendent, companion Fatima…”

“She has already conveyed this information as well,” I said. “Very good—let us visit the ‘Children’s Garden’ now, and the hospital after noon.” Just then, the sound of the gong rang out, and we made our way toward the dining hall.

On both sides of the street, the nearby houses presented a unique charm. In the construction of every house, full attention had been paid to strength, cleanliness, and beauty. As before, we washed our hands and faces and sat down on chairs for refreshments. On each plate were placed a jalebi, two eggs, and a gulab jamun. On another plate were slices of fresh and dried fruits, and besides a glass of clear water, there was also an empty glass, into which hot milk was later poured. As before, the meal began at the sound of the bell. Now we—Vishwamitra, Ismail, Priyambada, and I—set out from there toward the Children’s Garden. We learned that the Children’s Garden was at the edge of the village.

On the way, when I inquired, Vishwamitraji said, “It is not just betel leaves—many things have now been eradicated. There is no trace now of chewing or smoking tobacco, beedi-cigarettes, liquor, cannabis, bhang, or opium. The fact is, all intoxicating substances are strictly prohibited. Their prohibition was necessary because of their harmfulness; but even those things that are unnecessary have been banned by the nation. No item can be given to any individual without a special health-related reason. There must be one rule for all. Just as the necessary clothing allotted to one person for a year is the same throughout the nation, so too is everything else distributed equally. If betel leaves were to be provided, arrangements would have to be made for the entire nation. There are 250 million people in India. You can imagine how many people would have to be employed just to prepare betel leaves, betel nut, lime, and catechu for so many people. How can the nation today permit such wasteful expenditure? The millions of acres of land that used to be tied up in growing betel and tobacco now produce other useful crops.”
I said, “Your present national progress has found a single, sufficient axe for all vices.” Then I asked, “Now, Hindu—”

“There is no longer any dispute over separate feasts for Muslims, Parsis, or Christians, but how is the issue of meat-eaters resolved?” To this, Vishwamitra replied, “Now, real meat is not available at all. Artificial meat exists in whatever quantity one desires.” “And eggs?” “They are considered the most sattvic of fruit-based foods.” “So, are pigs and such no longer raised in Europe and America?” “No, not at all. Just look around here in the settlement—do you see any animals anywhere? As I mentioned earlier about the monkeys, through the same process of species-elimination, pigs, dogs, cats—all have been eradicated. Only for the use of students of zoology are a few kept and raised here and there.” “You people have given up the use of leather, so giving up meat must not have caused you any inconvenience; but with all this consumption of milk, surely many cows must be kept? Well, if not by slaughter, then by natural death, thousands of them must die? Isn’t their leather used for machine belts?” “Machine belts are now made from canvas, which is much stronger than leather. Separating the hide, tanning it, and so on was a very filthy task, which greatly polluted the air. Therefore, that work has been completely abandoned. When an animal dies, it is buried in the ground. Once it decomposes into manure, it is put to use. As far as possible, nothing is allowed to go to waste. We make full use of the bones, and dung and so on are also suitable for fertilizer.”

We continued our conversation as we walked. Every man and woman we passed on the road turned to look at me. The village, situated at the foot of the hills and along the river, stretches more in length than in width. In width, there are only five roads. The roads are quite broad, with dense trees planted on both sides. Along each road are rows of houses. The back of each row adjoins the back of the next row.

That is, the gardens of both are joined into one. In this way, there are six rows in width. The length of the village runs east to west. At the end of each row, there is a road running north to south. If a person starts from the village office, he will reach a crossroad where the guesthouse row is found. After that, there are the ordinary rows. Crossing three crossroads, at the fourth, one comes upon the ‘Assembly Hall’, which occupies space equal to two rows. This is attached to the village library, along with a large hall. From here, as needed, books are sent to and brought from the row libraries as well. Only a road separates the Assembly Hall and the Dining Hall.

The village’s new and large tailoring and similar work comes ready-made from the tailor villages and such, but even so, for repairs or urgent work, there is a place in front of the village office for sewing, dyeing, replacing electric glass panels, and the like. To its north, directly adjoining it, is the laundry, where clothes are washed and starched by machine. For drying clothes, there are large heated halls right there. Crossing one road from there is the warehouse for food items. Next to it is the parking area for vehicles, and the warehouse for other goods. Finally, for repair work, there is the workshop, where the work of blacksmiths and carpenters is also done. At all these places, only such repair work is done as is urgently needed; otherwise, things are sent to those villages where only that specific work is done.

In this way, it can be understood that all the village offices lie to the west, along the north-south road. The Assembly Hall and Dining Hall are in the center, while the children’s garden and the clinic are outside the village to the east. The roads running along the length are broader and lined with shady trees.

I wished to see the children’s garden first, but as it was mealtime, I turned toward the Dining Hall. When I was twenty yards from the Dining Hall, the eleven o’clock bell rang. Everyone, as before, washed their hands and faces and sat down to eat. The meal at this time was what people in earlier times used to call a simple meal. Bread, lentils, rice, meat, vegetables, curry, fritters—everything was there.

The food had been tasted. On my right sat Vishwamitra, and on my left, Ismail. We had arrived a little earlier, so there were still a couple of minutes to spare. I said, “In the meantime, let us go and see the kitchen.” The kitchen was on the southern side of the dining hall. We went and saw: for preparing every kind of dish, there were large vessels, which were lifted and lowered by machines alone. Kneading the dough, making bread—all of it was done by machines. Electricity provided the heat. Such a vast kitchen, where food for five thousand people was prepared, yet there was neither soot nor smoke anywhere. Every ingredient had its own scheduled time for being added or removed. The heat was also measured precisely. Thus, there was no possibility of any mistake in any dish.

Although all the ingredients arrived clean and pure, even then, until the experts in food quality and safety gave their approval for any item, it could not be used. I have already mentioned that real meat was no longer available; however, several substances were now prepared through chemical combinations, which tasted like various kinds of meat and had the same properties as well.
