In the kitchen, both men and women worked as cooks. The plates and bowls, once filled, were arranged on wooden trays, which, once ready, were sent into the dining hall by means of electricity. From there, two or three people would take them off the trays and place them on the tables. After the meal was over, the plates and other utensils were again placed on those same trays and sent to the washing room, where they were cleaned by machines using hot water and cleansing agents. The leftover food was loaded onto a motor vehicle and buried outside in a designated place, where it was turned into fertilizer. However, people usually took only as much as they could eat, so that little would be left over.

Before the bell rang, we had already taken our seats. Afterwards, we enjoyed a hearty meal together. After washing our hands and mouths, when we set out for the hospital, Devmitra accompanied us. We arrived at the hospital. Our companion Manorama and her other assistants welcomed us at the door. Except for one assistant physician, all the staff at the hospital were women. The assistant physician was none other than Manorama's husband, Mr. Rahimbakhsh.

Both husband and wife had completed their full medical studies at Takshashila. You are natives of Kashmir. I had thought that with a population of five thousand, the number of patients would be proportionate, but here I saw only fifty patients. I learned that, at most, the number of the sick had once reached a hundred. When diseases like leprosy, piles, syphilis, tuberculosis, epilepsy, asthma, and so on have vanished from the world itself, how could they be found here? Ordinary fevers, headaches, indigestion, some injury or wound—these are generally the only ailments. Manorama said, “Now, much of medical science is studied only for the sake of learning; this is the case with pharmacology, and the need for surgery is even less. Only the physicians of two centuries ago had ample opportunity to practice it; all sorts of new diseases, royal ailments, wars, and so many other causes kept their clinics ever crowded with patients. I do not regret this; if ever a day should come when there is no illness at all, how wonderful that would be! Even if, in the course of time, the study of medicine should disappear, there would be nothing to worry about. However, if on one hand the work of treating patients has lessened, on the other, there is now ample time for the promotion of numerous rules concerning health. In food and clothing, in living and lifestyle, it has now become the physician’s essential duty to strive for the inclusion of more healthful and nourishing qualities.”

Rahim and Manorama showed me every part of the hospital thoroughly. What can be said about the arrangements for the patients’ lodging and meals? Everywhere, there reigned a kingdom of cleanliness. The women attendants, with their sympathetic, gentle words and graceful behavior, dispelled half the suffering of the patients. The pharmacy was well-stocked. Useful instruments and devices were kept in abundance. After inspecting the hospital kitchen and all other facilities, we returned to the resting place. I thought to myself, many things from yesterday and today must be written in my journal. It is only one o’clock; I will do this work until then. Saying I would return in the evening...

Ismail and Priyamvada had already departed, but after escorting Dev to the resting place, I returned. I mentioned to Vishwamitra about keeping a daily journal. He too withdrew to his room. Left alone, I took out my pen and sat down to write. There was no end to the matters worth recording, but I was constrained by time and space. So, as far as possible, I resolved to write only the main points in brief. To ensure that no important matter was omitted, I decided that every night before sleeping, I would certainly write down all the noteworthy events of the day.

The next day, we set out towards the Children's Garden. First, we came upon a gate. Do not imagine the garden as some enclosure surrounded by walls or iron railings. There is no need for such things here. There are no animals to break in and cause harm, nor is there anyone who would steal anything. The gate is grand and beautiful; above it stands a two-storied building. As soon as we entered, we were greeted by our companion, Fatima, who had been waiting for us. Although she is eighty years old, she performs her duties with the vigor of youth. She has been a widow for twenty years. After completing her education and getting married, her husband, Shri Hrishikesh Dwivedi, settled here. Both husband and wife had been students at Takshashila. Her husband had taken up the work of a physician, and for ten years Fatima herself served in the hospital, caring for the sick. "Your love for children was boundless; that is why you later came to the Children's Garden. Since then, you have been enjoying the fragrance of these heavenly blossoms." Do not assume from her name that Fatima is a Muslim. I have already written that religion has now vanished.
Now we moved ahead. The garden was vast and stretched far into the distance.

chapters.title: The World of Children
paragraphs: It was as if not a single flower had been left out; every kind was there. Bela, chameli, roses of every variety, champa, juhi, mogra, kunda, and marigold—all of them. Many of the flowers were smiling, while many others, dressed quietly in their green attire, simply watched the spectacle. Here and there stood trees of pomegranate, orange, apple, mango, jamun, lychee, jackfruit, jujube, and guava. Vines of grapes spread across the trellises. In the midst of all this stood a massive pipal tree, beneath which the boys played during the summer. Although the sun had already risen, dew still clung to the grass, so the boys were gathered on the large, paved platform in front of their dormitory. The sunlight had reached there.

The women who cared for them were telling them that a very old sage was to visit today. Some of the older children—though none older than three, for after the age of three they were sent to school—would ask, “Amma! Is this sage even older than our great-grandmother?”
Then she would reply, “My darling, your great-grandmother had not even been born when that sage was already older than your grandmother.”
One child asked, “Then who is he like? Tell us someone from our village.”
Mother: “My child! Not just in your village, but nowhere on earth is there anyone that old.”
Another: “Well, maybe not on this earth, but there must be someone on Mars, or on Mercury?”
Mother: “There may be, but have you ever seen them?”
The second child: “Well, have we seen all of this earth either?”

Mother: “My dear! You will see it all. You have only just learned to walk, only just learned to speak. When you have mastered the ways of the world and the art of language, then you will see everything.”

Just then, another woman said, “Why are you troubling yourself so much, Vijay? Look, to the left of your great-grandmother, the sage with the white beard is coming. Look, pick up your sitars, each of you; today, you’ll see—”
“Who sings the best song for old Baba? I will sing too, Janaki Amma will sing, and Zainab Amma will sing as well.”
At that moment, Dhruv spoke up—“I will sing too.” At this, everyone burst into laughter.
Janaki said, “Dhruv! Don’t say ‘I will sing too’ like a girl, say ‘I will sing too’ like a boy.”
Dhruv, hiding his face in Janaki’s sari and wrapping his arms around her legs, said, “I will sing too.” At this, Rohini said, “And Amma, ‘I will sing too.’”

Zainab said, “Here comes another trouble.” Rohini was a two-and-a-half-year-old girl. Zainab picked her up in her lap, kissed her face, and said, “My dear! Girls don’t speak like that. Say, ‘I will sing too’ like a girl.”
Rohini replied, “Hmm! Dhruv Maiya was saying just that, then Janaki Amma corrected him.”
Zainab—“But you’re a daughter, aren’t you?”

Rohini—“Yes, I’m your daughter, I’m Janaki Amma’s daughter, I’m elder Amma’s daughter, right! I’m also Kamal Maiya’s sister. Shafi Maiya too, see, calls me Rohini sister—Rohini sister. Dhruv Maiya also calls me sister. So how am I only a daughter? I’m both a daughter and a sister.”
Zainab—“Alright, old lady! You are both a daughter and a sister, but you’re not a son or a mother, are you?”
Rohini—“No, I’m not.”

Zainab—“Good! So, if a son or mother says ‘I will sing’ as a boy, that’s correct, and if a daughter or sister says ‘I will sing’ as a girl, that’s correct. Not only that, if old Baba, father, or uncle say ‘I will sing’ as a boy, that’s right, and if old Amma, little Amma, or elder Amma say ‘I will sing’ as a girl, that’s right.”

By then, we had arrived, and the conversation ended there. All the mothers raised their hands in greeting first, and seeing this, all the children—except the very little ones placed in the small carts—also raised their hands.
To me, those children truly seemed like blooming celestial flowers; on their rosy lips and pink cheeks played the faint trace of a smile. On each of their faces...

Their bodies were clad in a kind of pink flannel clothing. On every foot were tiny socks and small, beautiful shoes. Each head was covered with a soft cap. As soon as the welcome ceremony ended, I saw that all the boys and girls—whom it was difficult to distinguish from one another—sat down with their little three-stringed toy sitars. If someone wore the mizrab the wrong way and it wouldn’t fit on their finger, they would turn to an older boy nearby and say—
“Mohan Bhaiya! Please, quickly put this on my finger.”

Murtaza once brought it up to his ear and struck the string, and a sound like “dim” rang out. That was all it took. He thought, “I’ll be the one to win this game!” Immediately, swelling with delight, he ran to Priyamvada, took her hand, led her a little way off, and said—
“Amma! Please, pick me up in your lap.”

Once he was in her lap, he brought his sitar up to his ear and struck the string again, but this time his finger was pressing on the string, so no sound came. He was greatly surprised—had his hope been dashed? Still, he said, “Ma! You didn’t hear it just now; wait, I’ll show you.” Priyamvada understood his intent. She gently slid his finger off the string. This time, when Murtaza struck it, the “dim” sound came. Overjoyed, he said, “See! I play well, don’t I?” Priyamvada replied, “Yes, my son! You play very well. Today, play for your grandfather too.”

At this, Murtaza asked, “Amma! Who is grandfather?” Priyamvada explained—“That old man with the white beard.” Now Murtaza said something clever—“Ma! Now I’ll sit quietly, otherwise Vijay Bhaiya will say I learned from Amma.” Saying this, Murtaza went and sat down in one place, making a face as if about to sing an elaborate tune, and began to pluck the sitar, humming softly. Seeing him, several other children began to do the same.
I turned to watch the children sitting on the carriages. Some were standing near their mothers...

One is sucking his finger, another is babbling “agoo, agoo.” Someone, laughing, is showing off his new possessions—his two front teeth. All the children were robust, plump, and healthy. Not a single one was thin, ugly, or prone to crying. I went up to a child of about six or seven months, and as soon as I reached out my hand, he stretched out his own, expressing a desire to come to me. And so it was that, seeing him in my lap, many others, one after another, clamored to be held as well. Altogether, there were about a hundred and fifty boys.

Seeing that it was getting late, Murtaza now went over to Priyamvada and said, “Mother! Shall I recite now? Why delay any longer?” To this, Priyamvada replied, “Yes, wait a moment; let me call and seat Grandfather, then you may begin.” After everyone had been seen, Fatima asked us to sit. Among the boys themselves, a little space was made for us on the floor. As soon as we sat, all the children gathered even closer around us.

There were thirty mothers in the nursery altogether. Each sat with her own child in her lap or nearby. The boys older than a year and a half had picked up sitars in their hands, and among the younger ones, some had a cat, some a dog, some a rabbit, some a whistle, some a doll, some pieces of wood carved into letters, and others had various toys—each his own.
Now the eldest mother spoke:

“Children, friends! Our grandfather has come here today to see his children. Now, everyone show him your talents. Grandfather Baba has come after a long time. First, Janaki Amma will sing a hymn, then Zainab Amma will perform, and after that, let’s see who will go next?”

Vijay immediately called out, “Me!” Murtaza had been ready for some time, but, caught off guard, had not spoken first; still, he quickly said, “Me!” Janaki took the veena in her hands and began to sing.

What can I say of the melody? Though the language was that of children, and the sentiment too was childlike, the tune, the rhythm, the cadence—everything was unique. From time to time, I noticed several children, deeply absorbed, plucking at their sitars and humming softly to themselves. Now Zainab took the veena in her hands. Vijay—her...
The Child’s World 46

The disciple was sitting nearby. He was already sitting attentively, but now, making a special effort, he stood up once, then sat cross-legged, just like Zainab, on her right side. In a sweet voice, Zainab sang a song. As soon as the song ended and Zainab set the veena aside, Vijay climbed into her lap and whispered softly in her ear, “Mother, shall I sing that song from the other day?”

Zainab asked, “Which one?” At this, Vijay murmured something. Zainab said, “Yes, my son, yes, that very one.” Now Vijay came quietly over to me and said, “Grandfather! Now I will sing a song.” Murtaza said, “No, Grandfather! First I will sing, then Vijay Maiya will sing.” Vijay replied, “No, I said it first, so I will sing first.” Murtaza repeated his earlier insistence.

Now, seeing that the quarrel would not be settled quickly, Big Mother said, “Alright, both of you brothers come to me.” Both of them ran and climbed into Fatima’s lap. Then Fatima asked Vijay, “That day, Vijay, when you and Shafi were with me, and I was about to give you a piece of apple, why did you refuse to take it?” The word ‘refuse’ for declining fruit from his mother’s hand sounded harsh to Vijay. He immediately threw his arms around her neck and said, “Mother! You’re just saying that; I didn’t really refuse, did I? I only said, give it to Shafi first, then give it to me.”
Fatima asked, “Alright, but why did you say that?”

Vijay replied, “Didn’t you yourself tell me that we should give to the younger brother first, then eat ourselves? Shafi is the younger Maiya, I am the elder Maiya, so how could I eat first? When Prahlad Maiya, Ibrahim Maiya, and Jamshed Maiya hadn’t gone to school yet, didn’t they always wait for me or Shyam Maiya to eat before they did?”
Fatima said, “Yes! My dear! You are quite right. So then, is Murtaza the younger Maiya or the elder Maiya?”
Vijay: “The younger Maiya.”
Fatima: “Then whose turn should come first, his or yours?”
Vijay realized his mistake. Laughing, he said, “Yes! Murtaza—”

“First you sing, then I will sing.” Seeing the elder brother and younger brother debating, now Murtaza’s mind also changed. He said, “Vijay is the elder brother, let him sing first, then I will sing.” Vijay replied, “Murtaza is the younger brother, let him sing first, then I will sing.” Now, seeing this new impasse, the eldest mother said, “Murtaza! The younger brother should listen to the elder brother, shouldn’t he?”
Murtaza: “Yes, mother! He should.”

Fatima: “Then do as Vijay says.” Now Murtaza ran to Priyamvada and said, “Mother! Please fix my strings.” Priyamvada took the instrument and tugged the strings here and there a little. Now Murtaza, sitting cross-legged with his right leg and holding the sitar in his hands supported by his left, sat in such a pose as if Tansen himself had descended. After a little pulling and adjusting, he said, “I haven’t learned the song yet, I’ll just play the instrument.” Vishwamitra and I said, “Yes! Let us hear just the music.” Now Murtaza struck a string with his finger, but his finger stopped short before reaching the string. The boys sitting beside him were about to laugh, but he tried again, carefully, and now a ‘dim’ sound rang out. Priyamvada, Fatima, I, and everyone else applauded him for this. Murtaza was very pleased and said, “Alright, now let Vijay sing.” Vijay, who had been sitting beside the eldest mother until now, got up and went to Zainab, saying, “Mother! You play a little, then I will sing.” Vijay had memorized one or two songs with great effort. He often sat in Zainab’s lap and sang while she played the sitar. That is why he now asked her to play again. As soon as Zainab began to play, Vijay started his song...

The sweet, innocent melody from the child’s natural voice filled every heart with delight. One after another, two or three more young singers displayed their talents. After this, it was the turn of the letter-players. Maryam and Rukmino came first. Priyamvada took the box of wooden letters in her hand and from it...

Placing one down, he said—Guess what this is. By misfortune, the upper line of the letter faced Rukmini, so that before she could think, Maryam spoke—‘K’. Now what could be done? Maryam’s joy knew no bounds. Priyamvada said—Daughter Rukmini, never mind, come, both of you stand in a line and guess this time. Again, Priyamvada threw down another letter. As it fell, both of them said together—‘R’. The elder Amma embraced them both. Now the elder Amma began to line up all the toys—dogs, cats, ducks, dolls, and so on—and said, “Priyavrat! Bring the rabbit.” Priyavrat quickly picked up the rabbit and handed it over. In this way, she would name each animal, and the children would fetch and bring them.

After this, the whole gathering rose from there. Even the very little children were included in this spectacle. The mothers held them in their laps. They went to the flowers and tested who knew and could recognize the names of the various fruits and flowers. There, many cradles hung from the branches of the maulsari trees; it was explained that the little children sleep and swing in these. The mattresses in the cradles were extremely soft. One girl would gently rock all the swings. We were watching this when, at that very moment, the boat bell rang. Today, arrangements for the meal were made on the green grass. Just then, many more women were seen coming from outside. These were the mothers of the children. In truth, here the word ‘mother’ refers to all those women who arrange for the protection, education, and upbringing of the child. Seeing every kind of convenience, even the mothers of very small children usually leave them in the children’s gardens. At night, mothers keep children up to a year old with them. During the day, if mothers of newborns work, they do so in the village homes, and that too for only two hours; the rest of the time, they entertain the children in the children’s gardens. The children’s garden is the playground of the villagers, where even the tender infants are included among the flowers and amusements. To listen to their sweet babbling, to watch their enchanting games—
Many men and women spend their leisure time there, drawn by the desire to witness it.

The aim of today’s nation is, indeed, to make the life of every human being joyful—and in this, it has achieved remarkable success. Yet the comforts and pleasures provided for children are such that even the princes of old emperors might never have dreamed of them. Generally, children are given light meals and food seven times a day, every three hours, day and night. Their first meal is at six in the morning, when they are served milk along with some seasonal sweets. At nine o’clock, there is kheer, some fruit, and similar items. At twelve, arrangements are made for rice and lentils, bread and vegetables. At three, again, fruit and milk. At six, more fruit. At nine, with both savory and sweet dishes, some milk as well. And at midnight, once more, milk and some fruit. The cycle of meals continues every three hours. However, except for three times—morning, noon, and nine at night—they are not fed to fullness. To aid digestion, the children run and play. Old games like hide-and-seek are still played. The boys play heartily with small footballs. Their game of kabaddi on the lush green grass is a delightful sight. In the garden, there is also an arena for their tumbling and wrestling. In short, ample attention is given to food, clothing, education, and physical exercise.

Indeed! The mothers I had seen arriving began to nurse their newborns, and many sat down beside the children to feed them. The mothers of children who could eat solid food gathered all the children, their own and others’, and fed them with equal affection. Truly, the narrowness of heart has vanished from the men and women of this age. Their hearts are vast.

Not only for the mothers who gave birth, but also for those who serve and care for the children in the gardens day and night, it is a matter of deep emotional pain that after three years, the children are sent away to large, distant schools...
The World of Children 53
are given. Yet, for the welfare of the nation and for the good of their own children, they endure everything.

After the meal was over, we all proceeded towards the museum of objects on the upper floor. Some children climbed up themselves by means of small stairs, while others were helped up by their mothers. Among all the children, Vijay was the most clever. His body was also strong and healthy. Holding Jainab’s finger, he walked along with us.

As soon as we entered the museum, we saw that various kinds of animals, grains, and other objects were arranged below. Bows, arrows, axes, billhooks, sticks, guns, pistols, spears, armor, and hoes were hung on the walls. Small cannons were also placed there. Above on the walls were large pictures depicting the life events of great leaders of humankind. Somewhere, Socrates was seen cheerfully drinking the cup of poison. Elsewhere, Buddha stood with a serene countenance, utterly unmindful of the blows from the bloodthirsty ‘Angulimala’. Somewhere, Gandhi was breaking stones on the roadside. In another place, Abraham Lincoln, undaunted by threats of adversity, was sacrificing himself to abolish human slavery. Somewhere, Joan was giving her life for freedom. Elsewhere, Ashoka, after the war, was turning away from empire. In this way, there were many kinds of pictures.

I was also told that children are taught many historical and scientific facts through talking films. The movement of the planets, the coming of day and night, the waxing and waning of the moon—all these are shown through them. All these lessons come to the children in the form of entertainment and play. The task of others is merely to collect materials that arouse curiosity. Once curiosity is awakened, the child becomes ready to endure anything to satisfy it. Then every fact is quickly remembered and absorbed by him. At that time, there is no need to force-feed or cram knowledge into him. While looking at the objects, I occasionally asked a boy the name of some item, or, by naming it, pointed out the object—
When asked to show, the children would respond with great delight and satisfaction.

Fatima explained, “The boys themselves take their mothers by the finger and lead them here. Sometimes they ask the name of an object, sometimes, upon seeing a picture, they sit down to listen to the story depicted in the illustration. They find more joy in seeing and hearing than the storyteller does in telling. If, at such a moment, mealtime arrives, they rise from there to eat with great reluctance. Although they are not given any books to read for three years, nor are they made to write, yet, along with knowledge, they come to understand many numbers, letters, and figures on their own, simply through play. They begin to recognize stars like Dhruva, the Saptarishi, and several others. Their vocabulary of nouns grows vast. Observing their mothers, fathers, guardians, and the surrounding atmosphere all using pure language, their own speech becomes very refined.”

After seeing all this, we were directed towards the children’s dormitory. Upon arrival, we saw that, here and there, swings were hung for the little ones. Soft, comfortable mattresses were spread on the beds for the children to sleep on. There were full arrangements to keep the rooms warm in winter. At night, very few children remain here; most sleep with their mothers. Those who do stay, sleep in the laps of their garden-mothers. Next to the dormitory is the dining hall. Beside it is the kitchen, where fresh food is continuously prepared for the children. Now, as the hour of eleven was drawing near, we could not observe the garden further. From afar, under small canopies, some statues appeared. Upon inquiry, we learned that there stood marble statues of the children’s chosen deities and historical great men. As soon as the children reach there, they begin clamoring, “Story! Story!” They do not rest until they have heard one or two incidents from the life of that great person.
Janaki, glancing at her watch, informed us that there were now five minutes left until eleven. We took our leave from the garden family.
That was all we were to see that day. The next day, from here, we were to go to Nalanda.

It was time to depart. Upon returning to the rest house, the subject of the journey—its timing and route—was discussed with Vishwamitra. Vishwamitra asked, “Are we to proceed directly to Nalanda from here?”
“We must go directly, but only in the sense that, once we board the train, we won’t disembark along the way.”
“Traveling by train will take a bit more time; if we go by aeroplane, the journey is only half an hour.”

“There is no need to hurry so much. Let us go by train, and, moreover, let us take the train that stops at every station. We should also travel by the same line by which I arrived, so that I may observe the changes in the settlements along the way. Since I am not likely to return here soon, my suggestion is that we travel from here via Raxaul, Sugauli, Motihari, Muzaffarpur, Patna, and Bakhtiyarpur to Nalanda. However, we must not rest anywhere along the way—only disembark where we need to change trains, and only for that purpose.”

“The train will only be changed at Patna. There is no need to go to Bakhtiyarpur; from Patna, there is now a direct line to Nalanda. There have been great changes in the railway lines as well. Now, not only in India but all over the earth, the tracks are of the same width. That width is somewhat less than that of the E.I. Railway of your time. Therefore, you will no longer find the narrow B.N.W. Railway, nor the ‘baby railway’ of Bakhtiyarpur-Bihar.”
“Vishwamitra! How do you know about the ‘baby railway’?”
“From reading books.”

“But you may not know the story associated with it; listen. You are, after all, a scholar of history. In those days, there was much ignorance among the people. In many villages, when a letter arrived, someone had to go to another village to have it read. When the men themselves were illiterate, what could be said of the women? Once, a rustic fellow was riding the train on the main line at Bakhtiyarpur. He saw, on the other side of the station, some tiny railway carriages, which stood before his own train...

They were just like a small child before his father. Never before had I seen such a tiny train. I asked a man standing nearby—who, though illiterate, was skilled in reasoning—what this was. He replied, “A baby train.” I asked, “Does a train also give birth to babies?” He said, “You can see for yourself; haven’t you seen a baby elephant? It looks just like an elephant, doesn’t it?” I said, “Yes, you’re right, the resemblance is striking; the only difference is in size.”
So, the poor “baby train” went on, along with those who spoke of it. “If the train doesn’t change until Patna, then by now the bridge at Mangama must have been built.”
“In 1650 itself.”
“Well then, what time should we depart tomorrow?”

“I spoke with our companion Ismail yesterday. He said we are to board at Mohanpur station. The people there are very eager as well. They insisted we stay as their guests for a night, but seeing your other wish, they do not want to hinder you. After breakfast tomorrow, we should depart at eight o’clock, carrying the final garlands from our hosts here. We’ll reach there by half past eight. After having lunch at eleven, we should board the train at twelve.”
“Very well, make these arrangements.”

Vishwamitra conveyed these matters to Ismail, and the same day, this information was sent to Mohanpur, as well as to the intermediate stations and Nalanda. Upon checking the train schedule, it was found that this was a passenger train, stopping at every station along the way. By traveling thus, we would reach Nalanda at half past six the morning after tomorrow.
Today, before breakfast, many people came to my residence besides Priyamvada and Ismail—among them Devmitra, Acharya Vishwamitra, and several others.

chapters.title: The Railway Journey
paragraphs: We all went together to the dining hall. In the assembly hall, the village had arranged a farewell for me with garlands of flowers. After refreshments, we reached the assembly hall. There, on behalf of everyone, Devmitra ji expressed words of affection for me. Along with this, I was presented with a poetic letter of felicitation, printed in golden letters on a plate of eight metals. The poetess was none other than Priyamvada herself. In response, I expressed my gratitude and satisfaction for the villagers’ genuine love.

Now, overwhelmed by everyone’s greetings and loving glances, Vishwamitra and I took leave of Sevagram. Ismail and his wife, as well as Devmitra, accompanied us in our motorcar. News of our departure had already reached Mohanpur by telephone. Outside the village, the Gramani and other respectable men and women welcomed us first and said, “All the villagers are waiting for you in the assembly hall.” Without alighting from the car, we drove straight to the hall. The beauty and arrangement of the houses were exactly like those of Sevagram; in fact, an onlooker might easily mistake it for the same village. Vishwamitra explained that, although the length and breadth of a village might differ due to limitations of space or variations in population, the layouts of the classes, roads, assembly halls, and so forth were identical in all the villages of the country. Some necessary changes were made to suit the particularities of the local climate.

Regarding Mohanpur, I learned that its population was equal to that of Sevagram. Here, there was a factory for making ice. Another enterprise was the distribution of fruits from the fourteen or fifteen neighboring fruit-growing villages to various destinations. The fruits from this mountain reached as far as Lanka and Burma. To ensure that the long journey did not affect their quality, the containers in which the fruits were stored were surrounded by ice on all sides. The motor vehicles used for transporting the fruits carried large, iron, latticed containers. Each vehicle carried just one such container. To protect the fruits at the bottom from being crushed by the weight above, there were additional lattices placed in between. As soon as the motor vehicle reached the railway station, the entire container was lifted by a mechanical crane and placed in the railway carriage. The railway carriage was built to such precise measurements that the loads from five vehicles fit perfectly inside. The counting of the fruits...
It is the work of the gardeners. In this way, the apples destined for Colombo (Lanka) are transported from Mohanpur and reach there in a single carriage.

Alighting from the motor and arriving at the stage of the assembly hall, the men and women of Mohanpur welcomed me with the same heartfelt warmth as the people of Sebgram had shown. The village chief there also expressed his goodwill towards me on behalf of the villagers. I too expressed my gratitude for this. After that, I was garlanded with flowers. Then, as it was time for the meal, everyone proceeded to the dining hall and ate together. Everywhere, streams of love and joy were overflowing. Due to lack of time, I could not see the other places here. The assembly hall and the dining hall were exactly like those in Sebgram. Upon inquiry, I learned that the children's garden and the hospital were also similar. The gate too faced the river, and a little away from the hospital was the ice factory. These things were told to me as we were leaving for the station. I kept looking in that direction, thinking I would see the factory's chimney; but I had forgotten that the work is done by electricity—so what need is there for a chimney, for smoke and soot?

We reached the station. It was already known that the train would be delayed by two minutes. Therefore, we sat for a while in the guest lounge, because Vishwamitra had explained that now there are no betel, bidi, or cigarette stalls at stations, nor sweet shops, nor the clamor of "Coolie, coolie!", nor the hustle and bustle of inns, nor the cries of hungry beggars, "Bless us, patron!" I asked, "Well, even if not, surely travelers must face difficulties without inns?" To this, Vishwamitra replied, "What difficulty? No one gets off unnecessarily. One only alights at the place one intends to go. There is no fuss over bedding or luggage. If the desired village is nearby, one simply walks to the guest lounge. If not, just speak two words into the phone and a motor comes."
At last, the train arrived. Today, after a full two centuries, I saw the face of a train. The line was broad, the carriages very fine, beautifully painted...

A new thing I noticed was that the engine was almost unrecognizable. There was no chuff-chuff of smoke, nor the overturned cauldron of black soot that used to mark its presence! The front of the engine was now pointed, shaped to reduce the resistance of the wind, but none of the old features of engines remained. All this transformation had come about because of electricity. Now there was no need to make steam from coal and water. Electricity was stored within. Some of it was brought in from outside and stored in cells, while some was generated by the very wheels of the train and collected for use.

In today’s world, where people debate the principles of economics down to the smallest detail, not a single bit of labor or material is allowed to go to waste. There is no chance that even a scrap of rusted iron, a tiny shard of broken glass, a mere rag, or a torn piece of waste paper would be thrown away carelessly. All such things are collected in the village warehouse and later sent to factories where they can be put to use.

So, the train now needs only a nominal amount of electricity from outside. The electricity generated by the wheels is used to run the train, operate the fans, provide lighting, cook food in the dining car, keep the compartments warm, heat water for bathing, and so on.

At the station, there is neither the commotion of ticket sales nor the stern rebukes of the police. As for the police, all I learned was that, along with the village council elections, a few people are chosen for this task. There is no fear of theft or such crimes. In a society so educated, people do not resort to violence or mischief without cause. But if anything does happen, or if a criminal needs to be caught or escorted somewhere, then these very people must handle the matter. In truth, they should not be called police at all. The term ‘sevak’—servant or attendant—used for them is more appropriate, for they are extremely courteous and ever ready to serve.

Since there is no need for tickets to board the trains, there is no longer any need for ‘ticket clerks’ or ‘ticket collectors’. Everywhere, messages are sent by telegraph telephone or wireless telephone, so the ‘telegraph operator’ is also no longer required. There are other employees to keep the lines clear and manage other arrangements on time. But now, ‘porters’, ‘pointsmen’, and station masters—all are equals—

In fact, everyone can do each other’s work as well. As for business, it goes without saying that everything is conducted in the ‘Bharati’ language. Since this is a central hub for the dispatch of fruits, there is much loading, unloading, and carrying to be done here. In this youthful age of machines, all work is performed by those very machines in whose veins electricity flows. Man merely gives the command.

A little distance from the platform where the passenger train stands is the goods depot, and just behind it, an ice factory. The platform itself is very beautiful, smooth, and adorned all around with flowers.

I also became acquainted with the station master. As soon as the train arrived, we boarded. Neither I nor Vishwamitra had any bedding with us. I saw many others boarding as well, but it seemed as if everyone had sworn not to carry anything with them. Each person had only the clothes on their body—no bedding, no covering, no pillow, no trunk, no water pot, glass, plate, or bowl, no hookah or pipe, no tobacco.

Truly, not a single familiar word like ‘matchbox’, ‘hot tea’, ‘kebab and bread’, ‘tooth powder’, ‘soda-water-ice’, or the like reached my ears. What was this train? They were like small, glowing houses with latticed windows. There was no sign of first, second, or third class—just one kind of train, one kind of bedding—call it ‘first class’ or ‘third’, as you please. The doors for boarding were set far apart. We boarded the carriage nearest the engine.

Now, as there was no delay, Priyamvada, Ismail, Devmitra, and the dignitaries of Mohanpur bid us farewell. The gentleman operating the engine had already been informed of my boarding. He rang the bell and set the train in motion. I stood in the carriage and observed: on one side of the train ran a passage, and on the other were benches suitable for sleeping, fitted with soft mattresses. I said to Vishwamitra, “Let this old man first see the train of your new world.” We walked from the front of the engine. Whichever carriage we entered, we were welcomed. Men and women alike sat on their benches—some reading books, some perusing today’s fresh...

Newspapers. The craze for newspapers has not diminished even now. However, there are no more advertisements for ‘banks’ and ‘companies’. Alas, gone are the phrases: ‘Ask whatever you wish’, ‘The all-seeing mirror’, ‘Genuine mummia’, ‘Money back if not satisfied’, ‘Earn a thousand rupees a month from home’, ‘Free! Free! Free!’ and so on. The newspapers no longer carry those grand, pointless headlines. Nor is there any trace of ‘special correspondents’ or ‘by Reuter’. Important news does, of course, receive headlines, but now there is no need to dazzle with external pomp to increase the number of subscribers. Newspapers themselves are not so voluminous as to be burdensome to handle. Thought-provoking subjects are reserved for monthly magazines. The daily papers merely compile the world’s daily news in brief. Each is published from the principal city of every province, bearing its name. Perhaps it need not be said that, as required, they are sent in sufficient numbers to each place so that every man and woman can easily read them. Once their purpose is served, these old newspapers are sent to the paper mills, where they are turned into plain paper, ready once more to be printed with fresh news.

The monthly magazines are lavishly adorned, resplendent with illustrations. Photography, too, is now in its prime. Not only does it capture the exact likeness and color of a form, but now even images are transmitted as they are, within a second, by wireless telegraphy to the other end of the earth, and appear in the newspapers just as they are. The very day I arrived in the orchard at Sebgram, my photograph was printed in newspapers across the world. Each branch of science has its own separate monthly journal.

By now, we had reached the railway library. Here, there was a heap of newspapers and magazines. Although there were two or three shelves of books as well, periodicals and journals predominated. Journals from the farthest corners of the earth on astrology, mathematics, spirituality, history, linguistics, psychology, philosophy, literature, electricity, agriculture, Ayurveda, botany, zoology, and other sciences were all present there. Men and women, here and there, were engaged in discussions on philosophical topics; elsewhere, they were expressing joy or sorrow over the latest news; somewhere else...

Some were diving into the ocean of literature, while others were simply reading or listening to novels; elsewhere, a music circle had gathered. After the library car comes the dining car. Here, travelers receive ready-made meals just as they would at home. Even during the journey, mealtimes remain the same. As soon as the bell rings, people prepare themselves and sit down on the benches. From the dining car, the food is served on wooden trays, which glide to their places by means of electricity. After the meal, all the trays are withdrawn electrically as well. Water taps for drinking and bathing are installed at various spots. The lavatories are arranged at the end of the train. These, too, are very clean; but unlike the trains of old, where waste would fall anywhere along the tracks, here there is a collection system, and at special stations, the contents are emptied through pipes. The purifiers are veritable water-deities.

Crossing the dining car, we moved ahead. Many people insisted that we sit, but I would reply that I wished first to thoroughly see the train of their era. Moving forward, we came upon a car for the sick. In it, five or six patients were lying in great comfort. Compassionate nurses attended to them with care. One was reading a book aloud to a patient; another was engaging someone in conversation to lift their spirits. On the nearby table, vessels kept warm contained milk, and close by, fresh apples, grapes, and other fruits were beautifully arranged. Two of these patients were coming from Tibet. Being chronically ill, they were being taken to Takshashila for special treatment. Three other patients were from different regions of the Nepal Republic. The physicians had advised them a sea voyage. With proper arrangements for treatment and nursing, half the patient’s suffering is forgotten as it is. When such comfort was once rare even for the wealthiest, what hope was there for ordinary people?

After touring all the cars once, we sat down at a certain place. At that moment, it struck me—here is this time, and there was that other time, when those who toiled hardest in the world bore the greatest suffering. Poor, hardworking farmers and laborers—even when they boarded the train, for them, standing room only…

There was not enough space even to stand. People were packed together like sheep, squeezed tight even in the harsh heat of June. In that crowd, sometimes a child would be crushed, sometimes a woman. After enduring for some time, people would say—why do you travel in such crowds, why not take another train? But by the time the next train arrived, someone’s court case would be ruined, someone’s wedding date would pass, someone’s relative would die, and someone’s money would run out. And even if one bore all this, who could say that the next train would come empty, allowing you to stretch your legs and sleep? This comfort of sitting and sleeping, this convenience for reading and writing, this carefree eating and drinking—where was all this available before? Even the pockets of the wealthy would be emptied while traveling.

Right beside me sat a middle-aged woman. Upon inquiry, I learned that she was a professor at Andhra University. She was returning today from a long journey after six months. Her travels had spanned sea, sky, and land. She had boarded a ship at Madras; from there, she spent a few days visiting famous places in Lanka, then went on to the islands of Java and Bali, and from there to Australia. I asked her, “Are there only white people living in Australia?” She replied, “Nowhere do only whites, or blacks, or yellows, or reds live anymore. People of all colors live everywhere. I know of you. I read your portrait and account in ‘Lhasa.’ You speak of the twentieth century. In those days, India was filled with many castes, steeped in feelings of high and low; similarly, in other countries too, there were selfish divisions of race and class. Where are those now? If, in our Andhra province, Tamil province, or Kerala province, someone were to recall the old days and ask—do you still have ‘Pariahs’ here, do you still have ‘Theeyas,’ are there still those ‘Ayyars’ and ‘Namboodiripads’ who would be defiled by the shadow of a Theeya?”
I—“So, do you mean to say that all these things have completely disappeared?”
The Lady—“Not only have they disappeared, but they have long been forgotten. Now, those things...

For the curious seekers of history, it now remains only in books. In Australia, or in any other place, there is no longer any old prejudice or stubbornness. Everywhere, guests from afar are honored just as they are in our own country.”

I—“I have noticed that you mostly speak Hindi, or rather, ‘Shuddh Bharti’ language. The ‘Ikde-Tikde’ dialect of your country had no meaning for the people here. When and where did you learn this language?”
The Lady—“For every Indian, ‘Bharti’ is their mother tongue. It is my mother tongue as well.”
I—“Then is ‘Telugu’ not the mother tongue of the people of Andhra?”

The Lady—“I cannot say that. People do know Telugu. For a long time, that is, until the year 2066 A.D., they insisted that Telugu should be preserved as the mother tongue and as the language for all practical use. However, since ‘Bharti’ was the useful national language of all India, one had to learn it; otherwise, a person would become like a frog in a well. People did not consider it wise to waste so much time on this double effort. Moreover, even before the establishment of the Universal Republic, the people of Asia had formed a nation and made ‘Sarvabhaumi’ their international language, which had an even greater influence on everyone. Now, along with ‘Bharti’, knowing ‘Sarvabhaumi’ has also become compulsory for every citizen. That is why ‘Bharti’ has become the mother tongue. The same is true even there, in ‘Tamil’, ‘Kerala’, and ‘Karnataka’.”
I—“So, have you built the palace of ‘Bharti’ upon the funeral pyres of your ancient mother tongues?”

The Lady—“Language is ever-changing. Is there any language that has remained the same for two hundred years? Right in our neighborhood is ‘Tamil Nadu’. The language that existed there eight or ten centuries ago was called ‘Shantami’, distinct from the ‘Tamil’ of your twentieth century. Without great effort and time, it was impossible for people of that era to understand it.”

I—“So, in your opinion, is the effort to preserve language and its literature altogether meaningless?” The Lady—“No, I do not say that. Language, too, should be preserved as occasion demands. Literature must certainly be kept intact. But for the sake of preserving language alone, the unity of humankind cannot be sacrificed. The task of its preservation can be entrusted to a few individuals of the race—those who have a natural interest in linguistics, history, or special literature; this responsibility should be left to them with complete assurance. The benefit to the world does not lie in fortifying many languages, but rather in removing the dominance of all and accepting one. Just as in other matters of welfare, people once held prejudices in the past. It was this very misguided prejudice that, in the twentieth century, had divided India into numerous communities, each at odds with the others. It was the same blind faith that led England, considering the ‘decimal’ and ‘metric’ measures to be French, to refuse their adoption, even though they were more useful and accurate. Now, there is no place in the world for such prejudice. Now, in all corners of the globe, the economic perspective is one and the same. There was a time when even in India, there was conflict between Hindi and Urdu. The time came when that quarrel was resolved, and the representative ‘Bharati’ language became the national language of India. Then, with great difficulty, all the provinces accepted the Devanagari script as the script for their provincial languages. In the end, all have now made the ‘Bharati’ language their mother tongue. The old languages are still read. Their literature is still enjoyed, but not with that narrow-mindedness. After all, not everyone is a devotee of literature. Those who are interested have every facility for study. How easy it is now! Through the universal language, I felt as much at home in Australia and throughout Asia as if I were in my own house. I listened to the thoughts of this learned lady with great attention. Upon inquiring, I learned that her name was Gargi. When I asked about her journey, I found that she had spent some time in Australia and, passing through Borneo, was now on her way to Nippon.

She went to Japan. I asked her, "What is the population of Australia?" She replied, "One hundred and sixty million." Many people from densely populated countries like China, India, and Japan have migrated there and settled. There are also people from the earlier-settled countries like England and others, but in such a vast population, their numbers are very small. This distinction, too, holds great significance for historians. For the people living there, however, there is no distinction at all.

I asked, "Did you also see 'Fujiyama' in Nippon? Was it not in 1613 that an earthquake there claimed seven hundred thousand lives?" She answered, "Yes." Afterwards, she traveled to Nanking. Then, wandering through several places in Manchuria from Peking, she reached Siberia. From there, she beheld the North Pole, and now, passing through Siberia, Mongolia, and Tibet, she is returning to her school. She has a great love for astronomy and geography. It is in connection with these two subjects that she undertook this great journey.

Yes, she was accompanied by two other teachers—one, Professor Haq from Vishwabharati, and the other, Professor Vishwanath from Aligarh University. Both these gentlemen were also seated on the benches in front. They, too, had greeted me earlier, but I had not realized it. The fact is, nowadays everyone dresses alike; unless there is some special conversation or someone introduces them, how can one know who is who?

Even the jails of today are of a very different kind. How can they be compared to the prisons of the twentieth century? Are prisoners here worshipped with curses and beatings for the slightest reason? Hearing such things, people today would only pity the intelligence of those earlier times. Nowadays, it is said that even crime is committed by man due to some mental illness; he should be treated—he should be given an opportunity to reform through education. How can those people impart education, whom the prisoners themselves regard as thieves and dacoits like themselves? That is why, today’s jailers are extremely gentle, learned in psychology and Ayurveda. For many criminals, even surgical treatment becomes necessary. Just as a patient is kept with care and tranquility, so too is a criminal. Punishment is understood to be only this much: that his former freedom is curtailed.

— does not remain. The food is just as exquisite, the clothing just as fine, and the arrangements for housing and education are of the highest order. There, under the guidance of such teacher-wardens, he reforms himself. Afterwards, he returns to his work. Just as nowadays the number of patients is exceedingly small, the number of criminals is even smaller. The fact is, there are neither rich nor poor; whatever goods, food, clothing, and household articles one person possesses, so too does another. When I have enough, and just as beautiful coats and shirts as anyone else, why would I steal? When all the delicious foods, for myself, my wife, my daughter, and my sons, are available to us without theft or deceit, why would I resort to such acts? Even if I were to steal something to sell, there are neither buyers in the world, nor is there any money. And what would I do with money anyway? For old age? The nation already provides attendants and every kind of comfort for the elderly, just as it does for the sick. Then, what need is there for money? For sons and daughters? Not that either. The manner in which they are raised like princes for three years has already been described. From three to twenty years of age, the nation ensures, with the same comfort, that they are adorned with the finest education. After completing their education, one may marry a worthy and learned maiden as desired, without the fuss of wedding processions, jewelry, dowry, and such disputes. Then, what use is money?

In this way, theft is impossible under the present governance. There is no landlordism, tenancy, or private ownership of property; all are national assets. Thus, civil courts have been abolished, and with them, disputes over land possession, quarrels, violence, and bloodshed have ceased. Excise laws, factory laws, currency laws, stamp laws, arms laws, and thousands of other such laws have been uprooted at their very source. Many of these things have vanished from the world altogether. Now, the only possible crime is that, over some matter, a quarrel might arise.
Both men and women are free. The bond of husband and wife is one of love; the husband has only as much right over the wife as the wife has over the husband. By virtue of being a man, he—

No one holds any special rights over it. Marriage, too, takes place only when both are young, well-educated, and wise, and only with the complete consent of both parties—without any coercion or lure of wealth or other enticements. In such circumstances, it is only natural that their love should be lasting. However, if cohabitation becomes impossible for any reason—or if, in haste, a mistake was made earlier—then even now, both are free. Both paths remain open. Both can dissolve the marital bond and go their separate ways. Society does not place any obstacle in their doing so.

Even with all this, if, due to misconduct, a quarrel, disturbance, or violence arises somewhere, prisoners for the jail are still found. If absolutely necessary, and after much warning, a person may be sent to jail for not following national regulations. In short, these are the three or four reasons for someone becoming a criminal.

By observing these and comparing them with the crimes of the twentieth century, one will see how few prisoners remain. It is found that in all of Nepal there is only one jail, with a total of fifty prisoners. In Bihar too, there is only one jail, whose number of inmates has never exceeded a hundred. Such is the case not only in the provinces of India, but in other countries as well. In olden times, severe punishments were prescribed for theft, the very existence of which depended on the flaws of the economic system. Those who, by exploiting legal loopholes, seized the earnings of others’ labor were considered great men and benefactors; while those who, unable to fill their own or their children’s bellies despite working themselves to the bone day and night, took a little from the hoard of loot amassed by others—just enough to save their own lives—were considered grave criminals. The fact is, the prevailing notion of that time was entirely different. A thief who, with a handful of men, robbed others of their wealth; a bandit who, with a hundred or so, plundered in broad daylight; and a conqueror who, with ten thousand, seized the homeland of others—all were given different titles. Alexander and a bandit, in essence, were no different; the only difference was one of scale. Yet, by the difference of scale, there ought to be something else altogether.

It was so, for one with small sins is a small sinner, and one with great sins is a great sinner. By this logic, the likes of Alexander and other great thieves ought to have been severely condemned, but that was a different world altogether. Far from being called thieves, people began to call them illustrious, mighty, world-conquerors, and universal emperors. In short, many crimes of that era were artificial and committed through force.

Our train sped along at a rapid pace. Sometimes the track ascended, sometimes it descended, and at times it passed through tunnels carved into the mountains. Even now, on the surrounding hills, there were orchards of many kinds of fruits. At last, after traveling for several hours, our train left the mountains behind. Now the route lay through dense forests. There were ancient sal trees, tall and thick. Here and there stood even larger trees. I already knew that in these foothills there used to be tigers, elephants, and many kinds of animals. I inquired about them. I was told that in these forests, there is no trace of those ferocious creatures. All the wild beasts have been exterminated. Their species are preserved only in zoological museums; a few males and females have been kept, and for their food, pieces of artificial meat are provided, which they cannot distinguish from the real thing. The elephants too have been captured and removed, leaving the forests empty. Their species has been nearly annihilated by this process of extermination. Now, only a few are kept for exhibition and scientific purposes. The forest is now free of all dangers.

We had scarcely traveled two or three more miles when we arrived at a station. The warehouses here were enormous, and from here two railway lines branched off into the forests. Upon inquiry, I learned that these lines stretched far into the distance. Not far to the east from here, there is a very large village called Paper Village, where ten thousand people reside. The arrangement of the settlements is similar to that of other villages. The inhabitants there are not deprived of any kind of comfort or convenience. In Paper Village, there is a huge paper factory. For all the tasks—cutting the wood, breaking it into pieces, transporting it to the factory, sawing and splitting, boiling and dissolving, preparing the pulp, making the paper, cutting, folding, and so on—electricity is used for everything.

Machines are used here for the work. From here, the finished paper is sent to the printing presses. At the station, I saw railway carriages filled with waste paper, decayed and rotten clothes, and the like. I learned that all this was being sent to make paper. It turned out that all the necessary materials for making paper—bamboo, grass, wood, etc.—are found here in abundance. Therefore, a factory has been established here. Beyond that, there are villages with wood-processing factories. In these, by means of machines, wooden planks are sawn and all kinds of wooden items—door frames, doors, cots, stools, and so on—are manufactured.

Now our train moved further ahead. I thought to myself that soon we would be out of the forest. But even after quite some time, I saw that the train was still passing through the jungle. Now, most of the trees in the forest were teak. I asked, “I haven’t seen such wood around here before.” Vishwamitra replied, “These are not just any trees; earlier, there used to be fields and villages here. It was a little more than a hundred years ago that this teak forest was planted. Now, there are many villages here engaged in making wooden goods from these trees. The timber and paper factories of this Terai region supply half of India’s needs for wood and paper. This forest has also helped bring rain and moisture to the hills beyond. The teak and sal wood of the Terai are very strong and beautiful.”

The train, stopping for two or three minutes at a time, sped along rapidly. Here and there, men and women, having heard news of my arrival, had come to the stations to see me. There was no need to get down. I sat by the window, and my long white beard introduced me on its own. When the train stopped, our conversation would be interrupted for a short while; otherwise, like the train, it continued without pause. Now we had come out of the forests. On both sides of the road, there were green grassy fields. I asked, “Are the grasses still green even in the month of Jeth? Have you, like other things, also brought the clouds under your control?” Teacher Hak replied, “Yes; now bringing rain—”

is now in our hands as well; when needed, rain is induced through science. However, here, from time to time, the green grass is watered by opening the water from pipes spread out in various places. Rain is made only to turn high, arid mountains green. Do you not see how level the land is, as flat as the surface of water? I asked, “Doesn’t the rainwater erode the land and make it uneven?” To this, he replied, “If the water were left to its own course, it would never fail to do so; but now its path is predetermined. No matter how much it rains, the water is directed through those paved channels or pipes into large drains and then into the river. Do you not see the railway road, with iron bridges built at every step? There is no obstruction anywhere along the water’s path.”

Now, herds of cows scattered all around began to appear very beautiful. Until now, there had been no wires set up along the roadside, but now wires were regularly fixed, so that the cows would not stray onto the path of the moving vehicles. The cows were very beautiful and large, the kind whose appearance one wished to keep gazing upon. The calves were separated from the cows and grazed at a distance. The cows were grazing on the lush green grass with great affection. I said, “Now what need do they have for grain or oil-cake?”

To this, Professor Vishwanath replied, “Even so, they are given oil-cake, maize, grain, and bran. As soon as they return to their stalls in the evening, they are served this delicious meal.” I saw in several places that long, paved tanks were filled to the brim with clear water. Water constantly flows in and out of these tanks. Here, the cows come to drink and bathe; everywhere there is the shade of green trees. Some cows were sitting there, chewing their cud. Among the herds of cows, several gigantic bulls could also be seen. Some were grazing, and some were bellowing.

At the sight of the bulls, a thought occurred to me, and I asked Professor Hak, “You people plow the fields with electric plows, and even the vehicles run on electricity; there is no need for oxen. To keep bulls, perhaps you need two or three oxen per hundred cows, but then what use are so many calves that must be born?”
Hak—How many calves? We allow only as many calves to be born as are needed for bulls. The rest are all made to be heifers.
Me—So, have you mastered even this art now?
Hak—Yes, as new needs and difficulties arose along the way, we worked hard and found solutions for them.

I said, laughing—Brother! You have achieved wonders in everything. You have made all difficulties easy and the impossible possible. Perhaps you do not know of a single thing that is impossible. These are the very cows over which, in the 20th century and earlier, Hindus and Muslims were ready to shed each other’s blood until doomsday.

Hak—Our ancestors are gone now, and it is not proper to say much about them, but truly, it was sheer ignorance. Neither side ever looked to their own lasting benefit. Gold was being squandered, and they were fighting over coal. Truly, nowadays, whenever we read about those old times, we cannot help but laugh.

Now I learned that the next station was Go-gram. I inquired a great deal about Go-gram, the summary of which is as follows: this village has a population of five thousand people. In fact, it would be better to call the settlement Gopal-gram rather than Go-gram, for not a single cow lives in the village itself. The village is adjacent to the station. The cows’ enclosure is a mile away from there. The grazing fields stretch for several miles. In these fields, here and there, are stacks of grass as tall as palm trees. Counting cows and calves together, the number reaches up to one hundred thousand. Of these, nearly half are milk-giving cows.

But who could possibly milk so many cows? Yet, just as science has made other difficulties simple, so too has it made this one easy. The cows stand in rows; thick pipes run between them, and from these pipes, smaller pipes descend beneath the cows. Rubber tubes attached to these pipes fit onto the cows’ udders.

is put in place. All the milk is drawn by machines and, through large pipes, is poured directly into the compartments of the milk trains standing on the railway line. The compartments fill up one after another and are dispatched to the villages where the milk is needed. Here, the milk is sealed in the compartments without ever being exposed to the air. Even there, it does not come in contact with the air. From large containers to smaller vessels, it is transferred through similar pipes. In the villages where it is consumed, it is heated by electric heat while still sealed. Only at the moment of drinking does the milk see the face of the air for a brief while. In the cow-village, there is no fuss about heating the milk or such matters. The people here are tasked with protecting the cows, breeding good offspring, extracting the milk, and sending it wherever needed—nothing more. For cows that have calved, those that have not, and for calves, there are separate grazing and living areas, from which they cannot come and go at will. In the villages of cows, buffaloes, sheep, and goats, a few horses are also kept. The herders, mounted on horses, govern their herds as they wish. The arrangements for the rest and treatment of sick and old animals are just as thorough as those for humans. The villagers come and do their work according to their assigned duties. The cow-village supplies millions of maunds of manure to the agricultural villages. This manure is regularly loaded onto trains and delivered.

The next station was that of the buffalo-village. The same grazing fields stretched on ahead. Just as beautiful and grand cows had been seen, so too were the buffaloes—impressive and splendid. Compared to these, the buffaloes of Hansi and Hisar in the twentieth century are insignificant. Their bodies were jet black. Their udders shone like bottles; just by looking at them, one could tell that if they did not yield a full maund, they must give only a little less. About the buffalo-village, I learned that there are as many buffaloes here as there were cows in the previous cow-village. After hearing the answer to my question, I did not ask again—what happens to the buffaloes that are more numerous than the bulls? Buffaloes are very fond of sitting in water; for this, wide ponds have been constructed at various places, into which water flows in and out. The arrangements for food, drink, shelter, medicine, and care are all just like those in the cow-village.

However, there are ten thousand people living in the Buffalo Village, each with their own specific tasks. The thing is, unlike cow’s milk, buffalo milk is not sent out. With the physician’s approval, a small amount of buffalo milk is dispatched here and there, but otherwise, all the milk is churned by machine immediately after milking, and the butter is extracted. This butter is packed in refrigerated train compartments and sent to various places. As needed, ghee is made from the butter.
“But, is the leftover portion of thousands of maunds of milk simply thrown away after extracting the butter?”

“No, there is a very large button factory here. The white solid part of the milk is separated through a chemical process, and from it, buttons of various colors and designs are made. Not just buttons—the same material is used for the white handles of doors, machines, and so on, so that they do not turn black when touched by human hands. On one hand, electricity has banished smoke from the world; on the other, it has also put an end to hands getting blackened. Today, do factory workers have darkened skin? This whiteness is also used to give gloss to art paper. Now, ivory is no longer produced, but this otherwise useless milk not only serves its purpose but accomplishes many other tasks as well.”

I had seen stacks of grass in many places, but nowhere did I find heaps of straw or chaff. Upon inquiry, I learned that although the stalks of rice and wheat, and so on, are cut by machine, the ears of grain are cut with a bit of stalk and set aside, while the bundles of stalks are tied separately. These stalks and straw are later bundled and sent to paper mills, where they are turned into paper. Green and dry grass alone is sufficient for the cows and buffaloes to eat.

Now, the sound of the half-past-three cannon came from a nearby village. All the people in our carriage came and sat on the benches. After a short while, our refreshment tray floated before us, gliding through the air along a wire suspended from the ceiling. At this time, the meal was something altogether different. In a small saucer, black pepper was served...

There were savory, ghee-fried snacks, fresh green peas, and tender green chickpeas. Each person had a glass of raw sugarcane juice mixed with milk set aside. In addition, there were some fruits as well. It became clear that people of this era are not deprived of the traditional delicacies of old villages. I was told that all such seasonal items are delivered to children and elders, men and women alike. During the season of maize, roasted corn would similarly arrive at snack time, had we been traveling then. Our compartment’s family enjoyed their refreshments. At that moment, I recalled how the Hindus of the twentieth century used to say about this very age that a dreadful Kaliyuga would come, and the earth would become hell. Yet, all these scenes appear more like heaven. Perhaps, to the selfish people of that era, the universal enjoyment of such pleasures by all the world’s inhabitants seemed like hell.

After washing my hands, I looked out the window before me. For miles, the lush green of chickpea plants waved across the lower fields. Apart from chickpeas, nothing else was visible. On inquiry, I learned that the next station was Shaligram. There, only rice and chickpeas are cultivated. After the rice harvest, chickpeas are sown in the same fields. Each bed, fifty by fifty in size, was surrounded by high embankments. Except for the finest varieties of rice—Basmati, Kisunbhog, Kanakjira, and the like—the cultivation of coarse rice has now almost ceased. In schools, a little is grown for preservation and educational purposes. For consumption, only the best rice is available. This Shaligram too is a village of ten thousand people. Besides agriculture, there is also a rice processing factory here. The work of husking rice is done entirely by machine. The rice is prepared and, from place to place, loaded into wagons and dispatched. Chickpeas are sent out whole, as dal, and as flour. The straw goes straight to the paper mills. Yes, the rice husk and other refuse are decomposed in pits to make fertilizer. The rest of the manure comes from cow-villages and buffalo-villages. In many of these animal villages, there are factories for grinding bones. As for the carcasses of dead animals, it has already been mentioned that not a scrap of leather is wasted.

They are buried. The decayed earth is later sent off to serve as fertilizer, while the bones are ground to powder in factories. Much phosphorus is also extracted from them, which is used in making matches and similar items. Although, with the closure of cement and the use of electricity in place of fire, the demand for matches has become so low as to be almost negligible; still, a few factories for matches have been retained.

Shaligram’s playground was right beside the road near the station. I saw thousands of men and women gathered there. A game of football was underway. Tall, robust youths were engaged in play. Oh! Just now, a goal has been scored—the entire crowd of spectators expressed their delight. Further ahead, a game of kabaddi was in full swing. On the green grass, players clad in shorts and vests were playing. The field was adjacent to the road, and as the vehicle had slowed considerably near the station, their strong, handsome, and healthy bodies were clearly visible.

Beneath the railway tracks, canals could be seen running here and there. Vishwamitra said, “Now you will not find the streams of the Gandak, Ganga, and other rivers as broad as they once were. The entire country is crisscrossed with a network of canals. A large portion of the water from these rivers is diverted into the canals right from the surface. Although the villages no longer require water for steam in their factories, there is still great need for it to keep everything green and clean. Villages with farms and orchards constantly need water for irrigation. Water and electricity—these two are the lifeblood of today’s world; indeed, even electricity is now generated from water, so water is everything these days. As great as its cost is, just as much care is taken to prevent any waste.”

As soon as we left the forest, the land became level. Now the mountains appeared far away, hazy like clouds. All around, there were plains upon plains. Only near the settlements were there trees; elsewhere, there was not a trace of them. In the fields, to carry manure and transport grain, there were narrow iron rails for small carts.

could be seen. Although the chickpea plants had borne pods, they were not yet ripe—they appeared completely green. Yet, nowhere were the watchmen’s huts to be seen. For miles beyond Shaligram Station, the fields of chickpeas stretched on.

Now the land rose higher. In place of chickpeas, there were vast wheat fields, heavy with large ears of grain. On both sides of the road, as far as the eye could see, only green wheat was visible. Swaying in the breeze, they seemed like gentle waves on a tranquil sea. What can I say about the taste of this wheat, or the whiteness of its flour? Yet, I had not yet seen the wheat grains themselves. I asked Vishwamitra whether these grains were better than the Pusa No. 3 variety of our time. He replied, “Pusa No. 3 is preserved in the school’s museum; how could it possibly compare to this wheat?”

I had already heard that all the work of ploughing, harvesting, and threshing the fields was done by electric machines. Each motorized plough had ten blades attached in a row, which dug deep into the earth all at once. The roller behind (the harrow) broke up the clods and leveled the soil. Sowing too was done by machines. All the work of harvesting, binding, and transporting the ripe crop was performed by machines as well. With good fertilizer and adequate water, the crop turned out exactly as desired. In these wheat villages, there were two harvests a year: during the rainy season, maize and millet were sown, and then this wheat. Nowadays, people eat maize and millet only as roasted ears or as a seasonal delicacy for a few days; the rest is fed to cows and buffaloes. Their stalks are also sent to paper factories. When still green, they are sometimes sent to nearby cattle villages to vary the animals’ diet.

In this wheat village, there is a large flour mill. Although it is not customary for every wheat village to have a mill alongside the fields, since there is no other such factory nearby, a population of ten thousand has been settled here and the mill established as well. All the flour and refined flour is prepared here and dispatched from this place.

After crossing the boundary of the wheat village, we began to see trees of mango, lychee, and other fruits. Upon inquiry, we learned that we had now come near Motihari. This orchard belongs to a school. It has already been mentioned that after three years, boys and girls are separated from their parents and birthplace and sent to school. Between every 30 to 40 villages, there is such a school, in which ten to fifteen thousand, or sometimes even more, boys and girls study. Arrangements are made here to provide almost all kinds of general education. Boys and girls study in these schools until the age of seventeen. Those who are exceptionally talented or have a special inclination towards a particular field of knowledge are transferred, even in the middle of their studies, from one school to another—where proper arrangements for that discipline exist. To attain the qualifications of teachers or specialists, one must go to another school from here; otherwise, generally, students complete their education here and then enter the field of work. The method of teaching, learning, and protection in all schools is the same. Upon special inquiry, Vishwamitraji said, “All these things will be seen with your own eyes at Nalanda.”

Now we entered the town of Motihari. Could the old visitors recognize it now? It has been completely transformed. The population is still only ten thousand, but where was today’s cleanliness, beauty, and uniformity before? After crossing the hills, we had entered Mall. Motihari is a district of Mall. There seems to have been much change in the names of provinces. The old district of Saran is also in this province. To its west, Kashi-Kosal stretches beyond Lucknow. After that, the republics of Kuru, Panchal, Matsya, and Shurasena exist under the same ancient names. Delhi is still the capital, or national capital, of India. Thus, the names of countries and republics have been preserved from old times. The names of places related to the history of previous centuries have also been kept as they were. Here, in the town of Motihari, is the office of the district council. The president and members of the executive committee reside here for the duration of their term. According to the origin and needs of the district, things from outside...

Sending and receiving goods and such tasks are among the chief duties here. Along with the district’s accounts and other documents, there is also a repository for old papers. Apart from this and the district office, all the other houses here are without storerooms. In the villages and cities, there is no difference at all in the houses, the way of living, or the food and drink. The old, decaying lanes and filthy houses are nowhere to be seen now. There is a grand building here for the meetings of the district council. The city dwellers have their own separate community hall. There is a printing press in the city. All the necessary documents for the district are printed here. The largest factory here is for repairing machines and replacing their parts.

As we moved ahead, orchards stretched far and wide on both sides of the road. For refreshments, I ate pieces of guava and jujube. Each jujube weighed about a quarter of a seer, and, marvel of marvels, there was no sign of a pit inside. Even in the guavas, one could search the whole fruit and perhaps find a single seed. What can I say of their sweetness and fragrance? Vishwamitra explained that all fruits are like this now. Inferior produce is simply not grown anymore. This entire orchard belonged to Ber-gram, the village of jujubes. This is the main occupation here. Fruits are available all year round, so the people always have work.
