On the other side, there is an orchard of jamun in this village. Here too, just as with the jujubes, magic has been wrought: the fruits are enormous, their sweetness and aroma incomparable, yet there is no trace of a pit.

After the orchards, once again fields stretched as far as the eye could see. Many of the fields had already been harvested, but there were others where, for miles, mustard plants hung heavy with pods. I learned that this was Telgram, the oil village. Here, sesame is first grown in these fields, and later mustard is sown. There is a huge oil-extracting factory here. Providing oil for food and for hair is the occupation of the people here. I remarked, “Then, even if everything is done by electricity, surely cloth must still be dyed with oil?” Vishwamitra replied, “No, first, everyone has a different outfit for work; second, all the work is done from a distance. Most tasks are performed by machines and pipes.”

I saw many wagons at the station carrying these oils, which closely resembled the old-time kerosene oil wagons. I asked, “Surely, scented oils are not produced here?” To this, I was told that the factories for fragrant oils are in cities like Ghazipur and Kannauj. For this purpose, flowers are cultivated for miles around those places. The sesame seeds are brought there from other regions, and the people there prepare the oils. In a similar way, I learned that there are villages dedicated to soap-making, where nothing but soap is produced.

At the next station, I saw a sign that read “Pickle Village.” Here, apart from pickles and preserves, no other work is done. For pickles, fruits and oil are brought in; similarly, the required ingredients for preserves come from the villages where those things are produced. Here, with the help of machines, the fruits are cut, dried, cooked, and pickles are prepared and stored in large porcelain vats in their big warehouses. When the pickles are ready to eat, they are then sent to various places in specially designed wagons that ensure careful handling. The people here are highly skilled in the art of pickle-making. They receive special education in this field. Pickles are made from jackfruit, breadfruit, mango, jamun, gooseberry, kadamba, and many other things. There are separate villages for producing each of these items. And in the size, shape, and qualities of all these products, science has wrought astonishing changes.

Further along the road, besides the Tailor Village, we came upon the Pulse Village. In Pulse Village, urad and mung beans are grown in the rainy season, and pigeon peas in winter. There is a huge factory here for processing these into pulses. All other arrangements are similar to those in other villages. After this, we passed through several villages, but in all of them there were only orchards of grafted mangoes and lychees. This series of orchards continued unbroken from Muzaffarpur all the way to the banks of the Ganges. Not only have the form and qualities of the fruits undergone astonishing changes, but the crops are now harvested throughout the year. Many trees in these orchards bear fruit twice a year. The seeds in lychees and mangoes are now seen to be very small; such fruits have even been developed...

There are some varieties that have no pits at all. The whole of Bihar is, in a way, an orchard of mangoes and lychees. Anga, Magadha, and Videha—these three regions yield the greatest abundance of these two fruits. These fruits are sent not only to other parts of India but also to Europe, America, and all regions of Asia. They are shipped in refrigerated wagons in such a manner that they do not spoil even after being stored for months. Mango pulp is also prepared; and the process and arrangement for making and preserving it are such that, when eaten, it tastes just like fresh mangoes.

We had scarcely gone a little beyond Dalgram when darkness fell. Still, I continued to inquire about and listen to stories of the villages ahead. After finishing dinner at eight o’clock, we conversed for a while longer. By now, the entire train was aglow with electric light. After this, I went to sleep. It was four o’clock when our train began to cross the bridge over the Ganges. Now we had entered Magadha. This was the city of Pataliputra, the capital of King Devanampiya Piyadasi. Once, as I recalled the scenes of my journey so far, I reflected that people of today are truly clever. In earlier times, every person wanted to produce all the things of the world right where he lived. Thus, each village tried to produce all the materials it needed. But now, thousands of people in a single village produce only one thing. The tailoring village procures cloth from the villages that manufacture it, and then prepares garments of various sizes for women, men, and children, dispatching them according to the orders received. Some of its people must cook food; but they have no concern with growing grain, nor with the price of flour or rice, nor with herding cows and buffaloes with sticks, nor with planting potatoes, eggplants, or cabbages, nor with crushing sugarcane to make sugar or jaggery. In short, all the other things they need are produced by other villages, whose need for clothing they fulfill in turn. Producing many things together with the help of machines requires less labor and time. In the past, people toiled day and night, yet the saying always held true: if the head was covered, the feet were bare; if the feet were covered, the head was bare. But here, in five days a week and...

Now, each person has to work only four hours a day, and in just that much time, all the comforts of paradise are made available. In earlier times, an entire life was spent merely for the sake of living. Man would toil day and night, and only then could he fill his own and his children’s stomachs, clothe their bodies, and protect their lives; it was difficult to find time for any other pursuits. Here, I do not count those people whose lives depended on the labor of others. In those days, how could a person set any higher purpose for his life, when he was constantly beset by such hardships? But now, the situation has entirely changed. Four hours of work; the remaining twenty hours are left for sleeping, reading, dance and music, good company, the pursuit of knowledge, contemplation of benevolence, service to literature, and all such activities. Even surrounded by so many means of happiness, one does not have to devote one’s entire life to obtaining them. What a system it is! By fulfilling your duty for nine months in the year, you may spend the other three months traveling and enjoying yourself; you may, with complete freedom and joy, roam any part of the earth as if it were your own home, by train, ship, or aircraft. There is freedom, too, in choosing your own field of work—only ability is required. Thus, an Indian expert in viticulture may go to France, settle there, and live as he pleases.
At Patna, we found the train to Nalanda ready and waiting. Our own train’s journey ended here. Bidding farewell to our other companions, Vishwamitra and I boarded the train to Nalanda.

Now our train was thundering towards Nalanda. It was early morning. Though the Lord of the World’s Light had not yet appeared on the eastern horizon, the crimson glow of dawn was already heralding his arrival. Over the trees of the distant agricultural college, this redness appeared just as...

chapters.title: Welcome at Nalanda
paragraphs: It was as if, in the dark of night, a distant wildfire blazed before my eyes. As though the sun, pausing just before its arrival, still hesitated to burn away the darkness of the world. Though the sun itself had not yet appeared, the birds, sensing its imminent approach, flitted here and there, perching restlessly. On both sides of the railway line, far into the distance, chickpea plants hung heavy with fruit, their weight bending the stalks. Here and there, narrow tracks leading into the fields could be seen, winding through the crops. I remarked, “Everything else is here, but surely people of today are deprived of the simple pleasure of roasted chickpeas.” Yet later, I found my assumption was wrong—I myself tasted them afterward.

My companions, too, had finished their morning ablutions and were seated comfortably. In the carriage, some people could be seen reading books, others were singing, while the rest sat quietly in their places, each absorbed in their own thoughts. Amidst that inner silence, only the rhythmic clatter of the train wheels echoed in our ears. Having completed my own ablutions, I bathed in the washroom and returned to my seat. Now, our train entered the grounds of the university.

Surrounded on all sides by fields, a beautiful three-storied building stood before us. A short distance away, a tall four-storied structure rose, enclosing a vast, square courtyard at its center, around which the buildings were arranged. Outside, the flowers bloomed in splendid array. Vishwamitra explained, “That is the agricultural college, and this is its hostel.” In the same way, other colleges appeared at intervals as we traveled on.

At last, precisely at half past six, the train arrived at the main station of Nalanda. The expanse of Nalanda is immense. Here, there are four stations, each named after the nearby college. This main station is called Nalanda, Principal.

Every train is equipped, along with other facilities, with a wireless telephone. At the previous station, Vishwamitra had once again informed the Acharya of our impending arrival. As soon as our train reached the station, the university sounded the bugle of ceremonial welcome. When we boarded at Patna, we had taken seats near the door, so as soon as the train stopped, we alighted.
On the platform, the Acharya and fifty distinguished head teachers stood waiting. As soon as I stepped down, all of them greeted me with a warm “Welcome,” and placed around my neck...

A garland of flowers was placed around my neck. Although a motorcar was waiting outside the station, I said, “There is no need for it for such a short distance; besides, it would be difficult to meet the children standing along the other route.” So we set out towards the ‘Vasubandhu’ building. On both sides of the road, rows of school students stood. These were all students from the higher classes. Each school’s students stood in a line at a designated spot. As we reached each group, the principal of that school was introduced to me. In this manner, at last, we arrived at the great hall of the ‘Vasubandhu’ building.

The splendor of the ‘Vasubandhu’ building is unparalleled. All around, as far as the eye can see, stretches a green lawn. The building itself is very tall, appearing as if made of white marble. Around it, beneath marble canopies, stand statues of many ancient and renowned teachers and illustrious figures of the past. I was especially delighted to see that here, too, a grand statue of Vidyavrat had been installed. This is the same illustrious man who, at the time of Nalanda’s revival, was the very first to give up all he possessed. All his movable and immovable property amounted to two and a half million. He had no children. He made the school his child and offered everything he owned. Vidyavrat truly displayed extraordinary courage and self-sacrifice at that time.

I remember that when the thought of reviving the school first arose in my heart, even I doubted whether a poor, unworthy person like myself could undertake such a great task. I earnestly wished that some great man, like Vidyavrat himself, would take this work into his own hands, so that I might follow him and joyfully devote myself to service in every way. But unfortunately, either the great men had no recollection of this important work, or they neglected it. Seeing this, and knowing my own complete lack of worthiness, I nevertheless took up the task. Yet, in addition to many scholars, a great deal of money was also needed for this work. There was no shortage of wealthy people, but many of them did not even understand its importance. Those who could understand, did not believe it could be accomplished.

Elsewhere, the possibility existed that by bestowing wealth and the like, one might be showered with titles and honors; but here, such a prospect was absent. In such circumstances, who among the wealthy would step forward? Though I had embraced the monastic life from childhood, I was unaccustomed to the practice of begging. This was yet another difficulty. Nevertheless, somehow or other, I steeled myself for the task. Enthusiastic souls began to drop offerings into my alms-bag. Yet, the same difficulty persisted. All these zealous men lacked the means to give in proportion to their enthusiasm. Even so, their fervor gave me great strength.

At such a time, an inspiration arose in the heart of Vidyavat. He was a stranger to me, and had never before engaged in such endeavors. Yet, I know not what sudden impulse seized his heart, for he sent me the deed of his entire fortune. Though more than two centuries have passed since that day, to me it seems but yesterday. Even now, my eyes behold those companions who laid their lives beneath the foundation stone of the school. In those days, we honored them—though not as much as they truly deserved.

Vasubandhu Hall is crescent-shaped. It has seating for one hundred and twenty-five thousand people. The galleries for seating begin before the stage and gradually rise higher and higher. Though the crescent of galleries extends far from the stage, they are so constructed that all, whether near or far, can see the stage. These galleries are arranged in three tiers, both above and below. There are long benches for sitting. At intervals, electric lamps and fans are installed. To ensure that even the faintest sound from the stage reaches the ears of the farthest listener, sound-propagating devices are placed throughout. These render every word audible. On each level, there are ample skylights and windows for the circulation of air and sunlight. The walls are adorned with portraits of the great men of the world, ancient and modern, and with maxims inscribed in golden letters. Most of these portraits have been painted by the students and teachers of the school itself. For the seating of both male and female students...

There is ample space in the building. To reach the seating areas, staircases are attached on the outside; only the path to the stage lies directly ahead. Beside the stage is the backstage room, where, during performances, the actors change their costumes and prepare for their roles.

The school community was assembled in the building to welcome me as a group. Therefore, the principal asked me to proceed there. As the time for refreshments was drawing near, he greeted me on behalf of the school with a few words on the stage and placed a garland of flowers around my neck. I, too, expressed my gratitude in a few words and said, “Now, I have returned once again to my beloved school.”

From there, I was taken straight to the school’s guest house. This guest house is a very large, five-storied building. It has comfortable accommodations for a thousand people. The arrangement of rooms and other facilities was just as it had been in Sevagram. However, this building is constructed around a very long and wide courtyard. To ascend to the upper floors, there are electric lifts on which one can sit and quickly reach the desired level of the guest quarters. There is a complete arrangement of electric fans and lamps, as well as water taps. Many men and women are appointed to serve and attend to the guests. There is also a large kitchen and dining hall for the guests. For swimming and bathing, there is a large pool. There is a suitable library of books, and for unwell guests, a separate infirmary as well. In this way, the guest house is like a well-appointed village in itself. At the door of the guest house, trams are stationed, which run to Rajgriha and to the various colleges spread out across the area. Whichever college a guest wishes to visit, they simply board the tram going there right at the door.

Seeing the school’s prosperity and advancement in this way, my joy knew no bounds. Much had changed since my time. Upon reaching the guest quarters, I found everything ready for refreshments. I took tea with Vishwamitra, Principal Vasistha, and the other senior teachers and mistresses. After refreshments, it was decided that today’s program would begin with a visit to the children’s class.

chapters.title: Education System: Infant Class
paragraphs: After refreshments, the other teachers had gone off to their respective places; only I, Vishwamitra, Acharya Vashistha, and the headmistress of the infant class—who was also the vice-principal of the school—Veera, remained together to proceed. The children in the boys’ and girls’ classes had already been informed. As we were leaving, it was decided that we should first visit the infant class. Exiting through the gate, we boarded the tram. The infant class was a kos away from here. Along the way, there were open fields, orchards, and schools dedicated to various other subjects. Today was a holiday at the school. Boys and girls could be seen wandering or sitting here and there. There were quite a few other people riding in our tram as well. Most of them were guests of the school; some had come to meet their sons, daughters, or relatives; others were here simply to enjoy their annual holidays; some had come out of curiosity about some branch of knowledge.

At last, the tram reached the main gate of the children’s garden. We got down. The staff of teachers welcomed us at the gate. The gate and the three-storied building aligned with it were filled with cleanliness and beauty. Besides the buildings inside, there was a vast garden attached, much like the children’s garden at Sebgram; the only difference being that, due to the greater number of children, this place felt like an independent village in itself. In addition to the sleeping quarters, there were a kitchen, dining hall, hospital, and storeroom. Inside, for the children to swim and bathe in fresh water, there was a cemented pool with running water, which never became stagnant. Here and there in the garden were fountains and bathing houses. There were large fields of green grass for playing. In the winter months, there was a large indoor pool with hot water for bathing.
All the instructors were women. Each boy and girl had to spend three years in the infant class. It has already been mentioned that the national...

According to the rules, all boys and girls, after reaching the age of three, are separated from their parents and sent to schools. The entire education is divided into three classes. The infant class begins at the start of the fourth year and ends with the completion of the sixth year. The children’s class starts at the seventh year and concludes at the fourteenth. After this comes the youth class, which lasts from the fifteenth to the twentieth year. In the infant class, the education is mostly uniform. Books are not much used for teaching, although the students begin to recognize letters and numbers even in this class. In the final year of the infant class, they also have to learn reading and writing. However, most of the education is oral. Every subject to be taught is made so interesting and is presented before the children in such a way that they themselves become eager to know about it. The subject in which a child’s curiosity is seen to be greater, the teachers also direct more attention towards that. As much attention is given to the intellectual development of the children, so too is their physical advancement kept in mind.

Although there are several wrestling arenas built under sheds for the students, where, at appointed times, these little wrestlers thump their chests and display their skills, yet, for the most part, they are made strong and agile through running and outdoor games. There are many kinds of games such as kabaddi, football, and others. The rules of these games are explained to them, and then they are left to organize things themselves. The teachers merely show the way.

When a child displays greater ability in his tasks, he begins to be counted among the higher ranks of his group. The reward for their merit is this recognition and the praise of their teachers. No other prizes are given in the form of objects and such. There are groups of ten children each, in which one is chosen by the group itself as their leader. Each group has its own golden room.

At night, when the boys and girls lie down on their beds, the teachers narrate stories of famous figures from history. These stories do not mention years and dates. Yes, it is told, for instance, that Ashoka came after Buddha...

—Chandragupta and Vikramaditya came even after them. The language of the stories is simple, and only those sentiments are chosen which children can easily understand. These stories pertain to history, travel, science, and various other subjects. Sometimes, the students themselves repeat them. At times, the teacher and the class sing songs together. The children are also taught the rules of health and cleanliness with great care. They are instructed not only to keep themselves clean, but also to maintain and ensure the cleanliness of their surroundings. It is clearly explained to them that their own cleanliness alone is not sufficient; cleanliness must prevail in their neighborhood as well. After cleaning their own place, they must never throw their refuse into someone else’s area. If they see any litter lying somewhere, they should remove it themselves or inform the appropriate person. They are taught to respect their elders and to cherish the younger ones with affection. The children listen with great love to the stories of those who sacrificed their lives for the world. The teachers narrate these tales in sweet and touching words. Many times, as they listen again and again, the children are moved to tears by compassion.

In addition to large statues and pictures, episodes from the lives of great men are also shown through talking films and moving pictures. The children watch and listen to these living, speaking images with great delight. In play, the children build houses, plant gardens, and hold councils. They are introduced to famous constellations and zodiac signs, and are told entertaining stories about their distances and related matters. The movements of the Earth and other planets and satellites of the solar family are shown to them in astronomy. Through these stories, a sense of brotherhood towards all mankind is instilled in their hearts.

Through the museum of dead animals and birds, many aspects of zoology are also taught here. From time to time, the children are taken to the zoological school’s animal museum. There, they are shown living creatures. Although in this way, the path to many branches of knowledge is opened for the children...

It is always kept in mind, however, that the children should not feel any mental strain in this process. Through these entertaining methods, they are also introduced to the basics of mathematics. Without ever mentioning the word ‘grammar’, the children are given a sufficient understanding of the purity and correctness of language within these three years. Through the captivating sequence of stories, they also, almost unconsciously, develop the ability to distinguish between the charm and dullness of language.

Within the kindergarten, the children have their own government. During the execution of its duties, the children display remarkable intelligence and cleverness. The students of the infant class wear shorts, socks, shoes, and either a coat or a kurta. In the winter, they also wear a woolen cap to cover their heads. There is no mention of any kind of ornamentation, but the clothes are always appropriate for the season and beautiful as well. In this attire, the boys and girls appear very lively and agile.

When we arrived, all the groups were standing before us, each led by their own chosen leader. The president and ministers of the children’s parliament welcomed us on behalf of the children’s society. At my suggestion, it was decided that we would watch a wrestling match. The children themselves chose their own partners. I selected ten such pairs. Among them were children from the first, second, and third years.

Upon reaching the arena, the first pair, both first-year boys, was called. Their names were Krishna and Ibrahim. Before entering the ring, they had already removed their clothes and donned wrestling shorts. At first, both watched each other from a distance, waiting for an opening. Eventually, they grappled with each other. The rules of wrestling were also explained—how, even if one is successful, striking or holding certain parts of the body leads to defeat.

In the end, Ibrahim managed to bring Krishna down, but Krishna was no ordinary boy. Even as Ibrahim tried to pin him, he could not succeed. While Ibrahim was still attempting to secure his hold, Krishna seized the opportunity and, with a sudden move, flipped Ibrahim flat on his back. The young audience erupted in cheers. Now both stood apart again. Ibrahim requested another chance. Krishna replied, “Brother Ibrahim! It doesn’t matter. I have already pinned you once. If—”
Children’s Class 61

“This time, even if you defeat me, we’ll still be even.” With that, both of them clapped their hands and the contest began anew. This time, Ibrahim truly managed to bring Krishna down. In the end, the pair was counted as equals. Afterwards, the other pairs too, one by one, displayed their own feats. Then there was a race and a football match. Some of the girls also demonstrated swimming.

Now we went to that side of the garden where the statues of great men stood. I asked Gyan, a first-year boy, “Do you know which one of these is Marx?” He immediately went and pointed him out with his hand—“This is he.” Then I asked, “What do you know about him?” He briefly recounted several incidents in a manner suitable for children to understand. In short, he said that Marx endured many hardships for the service of humanity, but never abandoned his cause.

Then I asked a girl about Darwin. She too, placing her hand on his statue, narrated Darwin’s story. In the same way, I asked questions about plants and animals. The answers I received were very satisfactory. Above all, what struck me most was that there was no trace of fear or hesitation in the children. After seeing the children’s sleeping quarters, I also visited the dining hall, the infirmary, and other such places. Today, the midday meal was also taken with the children’s group.
We listened with great affection to their songs and stories.

Their education takes place amidst green grass, trees laden with fruits and flowers, and in museums of animals and birds. Seeing the cleanliness, beauty, and fearlessness of the girls, I wondered—was the womanhood of the twentieth century anything like this? The male society had prevented their abilities from developing. They did not realize that in doing so, they were harming themselves as well. I said—among these children are also the descendants of those untouchables, whom people of that time, if they called human at all, did so as a great favor. Otherwise, they were considered worse than animals. There was no hesitation in cradling a dog in one’s lap, but heaven forbid that one of those unfortunate men, cursed by fate, should even come near. Oh! How many millions of such priceless human lives were wasted? Was there any limit to injustice? Even when there was a well in the village, those wretched souls were not allowed to drink its water.

This was not the case. And among all their faults, the greatest accusation leveled against them was that they cleaned filth—that they carried away dead animals, and so on. Yet, those who pointed out these faults failed to realize that for such service to society—for which no one else was willing, and upon which the well-being of society depended—they ought to be grateful, not, on the contrary, make them objects of scorn. Well! That too was an age of dreams, though that dream stretched on for thousands of years. Eventually, people understood—by belittling others, we ourselves must become base. May the world never again witness that dream, never again fall into that intoxication or slumber of delusion.

Thus ended today’s inspection of the infant class. All the teachers are of the highest caliber. Just as companion Veera is an ideal for the girls, so too is she a true nurturing mother for the boys. Having seen everything, we returned to the guest quarters at nearly three o’clock. For tomorrow, it was decided that we would visit the children’s class. After this, for a long time, conversation continued about the two centuries of the school’s history.

The Method of Education: Children’s Class This morning, we boarded the tram and set out for the children’s class. This was even farther away, that is, two kos distant. As mentioned earlier, the children’s class is for those aged eight years, that is, from six to fourteen. Within it, there are sub-classes divided into periods of two years each, each with its own separate residential garden. In the children’s class, the subjects taught in brief are literature, mathematics, geography, grammar, music, drawing, agriculture, cow protection, and so on. However, it is not mandatory for every student to study all these subjects. By encouraging a disinterest in greed for knowledge, and by observing the child’s natural inclination, no pressure is exerted in directions where such inclination is not seen. For example, upon entering this grade, from the third to the fifth year, every child is taught Sanskrit or some other language...

chapters.title: Education System: Children's Class
paragraphs: is the custom. The environment for teaching these languages is crafted in such a way (as has been previously mentioned) that the child finds it as conducive to learning as an infant does. There is no attempt to forcibly impose anything upon the mind. However, if it becomes apparent that the child has no interest in that direction, no pressure is applied. Upon entering the children’s class, the children are instructed in their daily routines.

As soon as we arrived in the children’s class, we were welcomed by both the teachers and the community of students. All the boys and girls stood in rows. Their attire consisted of shorts and a tunic. In winter, warm clothing to cover the head, as well as shoes and socks, are also provided. Each sub-class forms a small village of its own, where, in addition to the dining hall and assembly room, there is also a storeroom. Here too, there is a pool for swimming and bathing, and complete arrangements for gymnasiums and playgrounds. The building is three stories high. To ascend, there is an electric lift. Arrangements are made for reading, writing, lighting, and storing books. Upon waking from sleep, the children go for their morning ablutions at five o’clock. After bathing and other routines, the children have their morning meal. The four meal times set for the day are the same for the children’s class as well—unlike the infants’ class, where there are six. There is a separate school for instruction here. Benches are provided for seating.

Although, according to the rules, formal study begins in the children’s class, great care is taken to make the subjects interesting. At this time, the teaching of history is continued through books written in delightful language, through plays, and through bioscopes. The children themselves act in the plays. To satisfy their curiosity about science and astronomy, telescopes and laboratories are also utilized when there is eagerness. Practical instruction is emphasized in subjects like agriculture and cattle care, for which fields and cowsheds are provided. After completing the first two years in the children’s class, students are taught the universal language for two years. During this period, the subjects remain as before.
...continue in their mother tongues. Only the children reside in the Universal Hostel, where everyone speaks only that language.

What is this universal language? It is an even more refined form of Esperanto. The articles used in Esperanto have been omitted. Its entire grammar is encompassed in just fifteen rules. Gender, case, and suffixes have immutable rules, with no exceptions anywhere. For instance, there are only two numbers—singular and plural. There are three genders, but for all inanimate objects, only the neuter gender is used. All feminine words end with ‘a’, ‘i’, or ‘u’, and are used solely for living beings. Similarly, other vowel-ending words, when used for living beings, are masculine. For verb forms, there are directly four tenses: past, future, present, and imperative. Here too, there are only two numbers. The persons remain as they are. The selection of roots has been made very carefully. First, those roots which are common in Pali, Prakrit, Zend, and Sanskrit have been chosen. Now, by comparing these roots with those in Greek, Latin, Teutonic, Roman, Slav, and Celtic languages, those roots which are found in many languages have been selected. In the universal language, only words and verbs formed from these roots have been adopted.

Scientific terms that were already prevalent in European languages have been accepted as they are, only with suffixes added at the end according to their gender. In life, for national necessities or travel and so on, this language is greatly needed. Therefore, in the children’s classes, its instruction is almost compulsory in the ninth and tenth years. When I went to the Universal Hostel, I found all the children conversing in it. On that occasion, the ten-year-olds expressed their happiness at my arrival in this very language, many of whose words I had begun to understand. People told me that, since this language contains the essential seeds of almost all the mother tongues of the world’s inhabitants, it is easy for everyone. It is widely spread even in countries like China, Japan, Siam, Tibet, Burma, and so on.

X X X X X X In all regions of India, the Bharati language is now the mother tongue. Persian, spoken from Peshawar to Baghdad, also belongs to its family. The same is true of the languages of Europe, which are not only prevalent in Europe itself, but also in Africa, America, Australia, and other islands of the globe.

It has already been mentioned that the fundamental principle of today’s educational system is to assist the child’s natural, inquisitive intellect in achieving its desired goals. For this reason, after examination, the path of education is opened in the direction of the child’s innate interest. Two centuries of experience have shown that this is true education. The old method of forcibly hammering and molding children into physicians and scholars had caused many obstacles in various places. People of the olden times were indeed peculiar—especially those of the twentieth century. Just as parents, without considering the wishes and aims of their child, would bind a partner to his neck in childhood itself, so too would they decide that “my son will be a lawyer, my son will be a doctor,” and so on. The result was that, many times, the child found his studies not merely uninteresting, but more bitter than quinine pills, and no good ever came of it. But now, ordinary etiquette and useful knowledge of social conduct are acquired by children simply by observing and listening. And the pursuit of learning begins according to their inclination. Thus, children inclined toward mathematics and astronomy acquire in the children’s classroom as much knowledge as the M.A.s of the twentieth century did not possess in those subjects. In arithmetic, geometry, algebra, trigonometry, calculus, dynamics, and all branches of mathematics, they attain complete mastery. They remain constantly engaged with their subjects, with ever-renewed curiosity and enthusiasm. The subjects they study remain vividly present to them. The teaching of basic astronomy begins from the very first. Wherever, along their chosen path, the need for any branch of mathematics arises, they turn to it with great joy. Literature,

The same is true in the fields of language, history, geography, science, and so on, although no child remains entirely ignorant even of the basic knowledge of these disciplines. The reason is that they are needed in daily life, in conversation, in interactions. Since a basic understanding of these subjects is deemed essential for future life as well, children themselves make some effort in that direction; but if it does not suit their nature, they do not pursue it much further. In the twentieth century, as was the custom, only certain prescribed textbooks were assigned, but that is no longer the case. Now, which book should be given to read depends on the wish of the teacher, who constantly observes the nature of his student. Groups are formed of students with similar natures, and for each group there is a teacher who is an expert in the relevant subject. All the materials required for learning are available. In this way, the pace of education today is as swift as that of the airships.

We toured all the settlements of the children’s classes. There are five large villages belonging to this single class. In each village, all the necessities for the residents are provided. Elsewhere, as I had seen everywhere, it was almost a rule that houses did not have upper stories, but here in the school, all the buildings are three or four stories high, or even higher.

Each student has a separate cupboard for keeping books and other belongings. There is a vast building devoted solely to reading. For playing, wrestling, swimming, and similar activities, there are large fields and ponds. One can tell just by looking at the children’s bodies how much attention is paid to their physical development. After thoroughly inspecting everything, we also took our midday meal there.

By the age of fourteen, the girls acquire such knowledge as would have been considered more than sufficient in the twentieth century. Compared to the boys, girls show greater interest and aptitude in music, drawing, medicine, and literature. Seeing the condition of the girls, even those men of the twentieth century who attributed many weaknesses to womankind would have changed their opinions.

chapters.title: Education System: Youth Class
paragraphs: It all seemed so natural. Observing the teaching methods and qualifications here, I became convinced that many of the blessings enjoyed by the human world today are owed to this very system. On one hand, the root of thousands of disputes and hardships—mutual inequality—had been eliminated, and on the other, there was such an all-encompassing, virtuous education; then why should not the world of humans surpass even the imagined heavens of old?

As before, I continued to inspect one or two departments of the school each day. After doing this for twelve days, I was able to take a cursory look at all of them. The education in the infant and children’s classes covers many subjects (though the natural inclinations of the students are always given full consideration), but such a mixed curriculum does not exist in the youth class. To ensure the smooth functioning of worldly affairs, and also because of the natural curiosity of human beings, the first two classes provide a somewhat all-encompassing education. However, for those entering the youth class, there are numerous schools, each dedicated to a particular branch of knowledge. Now, the student studies only that subject toward which his natural inclination lies, and which he has already studied primarily—giving lesser attention to others—in previous years. Although such students are very few, there are indeed some who remain ignorant of practical knowledge, simply because, lacking interest, they are not compelled to exert themselves in that direction.

At Nalanda University, there are fifteen separate schools for different subjects, renowned by the names of Language-Archaeology, Astronomy, Philosophy, Science, Literature, Music, Painting, Architecture (Civil Engineering), Ayurveda, Botany, Zoology, Agriculture, Mechanical Engineering, and Education. The teachers are experts in their respective fields. In the Language-Archaeology school, students are introduced to the primary sources of history and their...

The methods of collecting are now described. This is not the twentieth century, but the twenty-second. Materials lying beneath the earth, sand, or the oceans have been found here in abundance. Much light has been shed upon the religions, customs, and histories of many ancient peoples. Numerous artifacts indicative of the ancient civilizations of India, Egypt, Assyria, Chaldea, Iran, Mexico, Brazil, and many other countries have come into our hands. The nation has spared no effort in acquiring and preserving these materials. Where hundreds of thousands of people are engaged in excavating ancient ruins and constructing secure places for the protection of these objects, thousands of scholars are laboring day and night to unravel their mysteries.

For the ancient civilization and history of India, searches have been carried out as far as Central Asia, Tibet, the Himalayas, Java, Bali, Siam, Sumatra, and Lanka (Ceylon). In this endeavor, the Nalanda University has played the most significant—indeed, the central—role. Alongside the School of Archaeology, there is here a vast museum of these historical materials; it contains not only relics of ancient India, but also artifacts from the histories of Assyria, Egypt, Mexico, and other lands. Replicas of objects of this kind, found in other museums of the world, are also kept here. Many ancient objects belonging to Nalanda University itself have been collected here. The historical materials that had previously gone to other museums have now been returned here as well. The museum building, eight stories tall, stretches over a great distance.

The new method of language instruction is so simple that it has removed many further difficulties. Students with a fundamental curiosity for archaeology and history are first taught the languages required for their chosen fields.

The School of Astronomy is in Rajgriha. Attached to it is a vast observatory, built upon the 'Baibhara Giri' there. Baibhara Giri has been utterly transformed. There is now an excellent road leading up, lined on both sides with trees. The observatory houses many telescopes, one of which is among the three largest in the world. With it, the phenomena of the planets, ordinarily observed...

The figure appears magnified millions of times. In the same way, the spectroscope is also an instrument of immense power. The wireless telegraphy station here is a major hub. Now, much more is known about Mars. There, conversations have begun just as they do on Earth, from one place to another. At first, there was difficulty in understanding each other’s languages, but now even that has been overcome. Although, day by day, the scarcity of rain and water increases, and the Martian core’s warmth—the vital force of life—continues to diminish, causing the people there much concern, they have nevertheless devised many solutions. On one hand, they have laid out a network of canals; on the other, they have curbed population growth—not only curbed it, but have actually begun to reduce it. Although people are striving to reach a new planet, no means for this has yet been found. The people of Earth, too, seeing their difficulties, have not remained silent. They too are searching for a solution. Some have even begun to prophesy that the time is near when humans will be able to travel from one planet to another. If this becomes possible, our world of living and our bonds of brotherhood will grow even stronger. As each planet cools, people will be able to move in advance to another planet. On Baibhargiri, houses have been built far and wide solely for the work of the observatory. With excellent arrangements for water and electricity above, it has become an even more delightful place.

The School of Philosophy lies two kos behind here. Not only are Indian theistic and atheistic philosophies taught here, but also the philosophical thoughts of the entire world are studied and taught. Acharya Vasistha himself is an extraordinary scholar in this field. Much of his time is spent in its study and teaching. All the schools are situated far apart from each other. Between them lie either open fields or orchards of mangoes, lychees, and other fruits stretching for miles. All the schools are equipped with libraries and all necessary materials. Where the School of Science is adorned with a chemistry lab and experimental laboratories, the schools of botany and zoology have, along with them, large...

There are botanical gardens and zoological museums. In this way, all the schools are imparting comprehensive education. Right beside them are the hostels for each of these schools. What are these hostels? Each is like a village in itself. The hostels and schools for boys and girls are together. The distinction between male and female has been all but abolished.

In the school settlements, some people are appointed for cooking, cleanliness, and the maintenance of machines and such; their residences are in separate settlements. There are also separate villages for washing boys’ clothes and for sewing garments. Similarly, there is a cattle-tending village nearby, though outside the boundary of the school. The ‘Nalanda Press,’ which was originally established for printing books, now has much more work. Several monthly journals on various sciences are published from here.

The ancient stupas and buildings of Nalanda have been completely preserved. The statue of Buddha, once famous among the rural folk of the twentieth century as Bhairavji, now has a very fine canopy over it. That colossal, beautiful, serene statue now appears even more enchanting. The large stupa beside it now looks almost new. The village of Suryanarayan and the settlement near it are no longer there.

In the advanced classes of the school, and among the specialists who have completed their education and wish to study further, there are now a great many students from outside India—Lanka, Burma, Siam, Java, China, Japan, Tibet, and other countries. Among the teachers of these lands, there is nowadays a considerable number educated at Nalanda. There is no branch of knowledge in the world whose higher education is not imparted at this school. Perhaps there is hardly a corner of the world where a student of Nalanda is not found.
While living in Nalanda and carrying out my work, I thought it proper to acquaint myself with the current system of governance as well. In this task, Upadhyaya Vishwa—

chapters.title: System of Governance
paragraphs: My friend gave great assistance. From the description so far, it must have become clear that now, everywhere on the globe, equality reigns. The oppressions that once prevailed in the name of religion, in the name of Brahmin-Rajput-Sheikh-Sayyid castes, in the name of wealth and power, in the name of white and black—how many human beings were crushed under the feet of others for their entire lives—now, even their names are forgotten. Now, man is equal to man, woman is equal to man. Everywhere, the principle of equality in labor and enjoyment is the fundamental mantra. There are no landlords left on earth; no wealthy merchants or moneylenders; no kings, no subjects; no rich, no poor; no high, no low. All the inhabitants of the globe form a single family. All the movable and immovable property of the earth belongs to this family. For the fulfillment of daily necessities, everyone, according to their ability, strives diligently for the production and collection of whatever materials are required. To reduce labor and increase production, the tasks and labors have been divided into many departments. To the people of the twentieth century, the divisions of today might seem strange. Now, perhaps not a single village can produce even one essential item of life without the help of another. Where once a village, besides growing various kinds of grains and vegetables, also engaged in many small crafts, today there is this remarkable village, which, though many times larger in size, population, and expenditure, does not produce a single thing entirely by itself. If it grows wheat, the flour is milled elsewhere; if it grows sugarcane, the sugar is made elsewhere; if it produces milk, the fodder and grain are brought from another place; if it does tailoring, the cloth must be procured from elsewhere. As for the casting and repair of machines, that used to be done elsewhere even before. The entire human society of today is so abundantly supplied with the necessities of life that, had this not been done, it would have required much more time. Today, by working only four hours a day, a person is able to obtain all necessities and spend the remaining twenty hours enjoying the other pleasures of life—when could this ever have been possible before? If machines had not been put to use,

It was impossible to attain such enjoyment, even if all of one’s time were devoted solely to it. The division of labor has also proved beneficial in making the use of machines more advantageous. Some division of labor had existed before as well, but people of the present day have applied this principle in an even broader sense.
In earlier governments, the proportion of destructive activities was greater than that of constructive ones. Whenever a war broke out, it was as if a volcano of destruction erupted.

Before saying more on this subject, it seems appropriate to mention something about the structure of the current system of governance. The basic framework of governance across the globe can be understood by looking at the system of village administration. The village governing assembly—or, in short, the village assembly—has the right to elect one representative (panch) for every hundred people in its population. If a village has five thousand people, then its village assembly will have fifty members. In this election, every man and woman of the village is equally eligible to vote and to stand as a candidate, provided that no mental or physical incapacity stands in the way. These assembly members then elect their own president or head of the village, as well as a working committee of sixteen members.

The responsibility for overseeing and managing the needs and production of the village rests in the hands of this executive committee. It has already been mentioned once that each category or section of the village has a leader. This leader is chosen by a hundred families, which may include up to two hundred individuals. There may be fewer than two hundred, as some men and women might be unmarried. The village executive committee delegates much of its work to these leaders. In times of disturbance or other necessity, it is the duty of all to assist the governing assembly, but at such times, the primary responsibility falls upon these leaders. The work once performed by the police in earlier times is now carried out by them. If, for any reason, one is absent from duty, then in their place—

In the villages, assistant leaders perform their duties. Assigning the various villagers to different tasks, according to the consent of the village assembly, is the responsibility of the executive committee. As needed, it appoints the heads of all departments, such as the physician, gardener, librarian, steward of meals, storekeeper, and others. The term of the elected members of the village assembly is, at most, three years. This same term applies to the members of the Universal Assembly as well. However, this rule does not apply to those chosen for educational institutions. Thus, any teacher has the right to remain in his position for life, provided he has not committed any unforgivable offense in the eyes of the people.

After the villages, several villages were once grouped together to form tehsil or sub-division assemblies, and in some places, police station assemblies. But these have been dissolved for over a hundred years. Due to the excellent management of the villages, the presence of electric vehicles, and the superb arrangement of telephones in every village, the distance to the district is now practically the same as that to the former tehsil. Just as one member is elected to the village assembly for every hundred people, so too, one person is elected to the district governing assembly for every twenty thousand people. For example, in Patna district, there are one million inhabitants, and its governing assembly consists of fifty members. For every five members, one is chosen for the executive committee. Thus, the executive committee of Patna district comprises ten members, in whose hands rest the following ten departments:

1—Education; 2—Health, population regulation; 3—Peace and order, justice; 4—Finance; 5—Relations and transactions with other districts and places; 6—Agriculture, crafts and industries; 7—Construction and improvement of machinery, workshops, etc.; 8—Post, telegraph, railways, aviation;
6—Archaeology-History-Preservation; 10—Press.

Before the elections, the names of candidates are proposed by the village assemblies of the district and the general public. These names are published prior to the election date for the awareness and consideration of the people. Afterwards, on a single day and at the same time in every village, votes are cast regarding these candidates; then, the names of the men and women elected by majority consensus are announced. If any member is found unfit in any way, the electors have the right to remove that representative from office. Each member is elected from a separate, distinct constituency. In Patna, there are fifty such constituencies. The main occupation of the people in the district headquarters is to carry out tasks related to district administration. The work of writing, printing, preserving old documents, and the various administrative departments—all are conducted there. Although every third year the members of the district administrative council are changed, the workers of the various departments and other officials remain as before. The council members of the executive committee reside at the principal place of the district for the duration of their term.

The functions of the first and second departments of the district are clear from their names. The Department of Peace, Order, and Justice is responsible for maintaining peace, running the courts, and administering proper punishment and reform to offenders. Since no one now possesses any private property, the term "civil court" has become obsolete. Therefore, when one speaks of the court, only the criminal court is to be understood. Just as shops have disappeared from the world, so too has the government’s sale of stamps, the betel and areca nut for the clerks, and the lawyers’ fees. Of that once-prestigious profession of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, there is now no trace at all. The courtroom is a spacious hall, where at least two learned, elderly, and experienced judges preside. Every case comes through the village’s justice council—a committee organized by the village assembly—where either the village assembly itself delivers a verdict...

...remains, or after an initial investigation, submits the case to the district court. The plaintiff, defendant, and witnesses are all present. The judge himself strives to reach the depths of every matter. The number of prosecutions is extremely low, so there is no bustle in the courts. Cases are resolved under just three categories: insult, assault, or murder. The punishment of hanging or capital punishment has now been completely abolished; in its place, criminals are kept on some island, deprived of the joys of human society, where proper arrangements are made for their treatment, education, and so on. However, when it is established that their nature has changed and they are no longer dangerous to society, they are released. For other crimes, each province must maintain a jail, where offenders are kept and reformed.

Through the fifth department, goods produced in the district are sent to external places where they are needed, and necessary items are imported from other districts and provinces. This is, in a way, the gateway for the exchange of goods within and outside the district. The functions of the remaining departments are clear from their names.

Above several districts is the provincial governing assembly. For every two hundred thousand people, one member is elected to this assembly. The method of nomination before election is the same from the bottom up. In Bihar, there are twenty million men and women eligible to vote. Thus, the provincial assembly here has one hundred members. Its executive committee, as before, consists of ten members or ministers from the ten departments. Their functions are also as before, but the area is broader. The provincial court is the final place for appeals. Here too, it is required that the executive members and the president reside at the provincial headquarters for the duration of their term. Other assembly members come only during the sessions.

Above the provinces is the national assembly. For this, one representative is elected for every one hundred thousand people. In India at this time, there are two hundred million men and women eligible to vote; the remaining fifty million are under twenty years of age or are students.

In the executive council of the Indian government, there are likewise ten members, who are required to reside in Delhi for the duration of their term. However, unlike two centuries ago, these poor fellows are not blessed with the privilege of a summer retreat in Shimla. The departments remain as before, but the scope of work has greatly expanded.

Above this is the Universal Assembly, for which one representative is elected for every five million people. At present, the population of the globe is one billion, eighty-eight crores, of which thirty-eight crores are students and the like; the remaining one and a half billion men and women are eligible voters. Out of the three hundred members of the Universal Assembly, forty are sent by India. The executive council of the Universal Assembly consists of fifteen secretaries. The president of the Universal Assembly is called the President. The seat of the Universal Assembly is on the banks of the Narang River in the country of Brazil, South America, precisely on the equator. Here, the latitude is considered zero. The name of this city is Universal City. It has now been a hundred years since it was founded. On the very day the Universal Government was established, a Universal Era was also inaugurated. At present, the year 101 of this era is running. The members of the Universal Assembly travel by airships. The President and the members or secretaries of the executive council reside in Universal City for the duration of their term. The proceedings of the Universal Assembly are conducted in the Universal Language. Fifty thousand men and women live in Universal City. Among them are people from all countries, appointed in the various departmental offices and engaged in other duties. The Universal Secretaries are in charge of the following departments:
1—Education 2—Health 3—Peace and Order 4—Finance 5—Trade and Exchange 6—Agriculture 7—Industry and Vocations 8—Machinery
6. House and Road Construction, etc. 10. Post and Telegraph 11. Vehicles and Aircraft 12. Printing 13. Population Control 14. Archaeological Museum 15. Recorded History

Great efforts have been made in the past two centuries to prevent the excessive increase of the human population, and these efforts have met with complete success. This department is connected from the highest level down to the village. Every ten years, a population census is conducted, but in addition to this, whenever a pregnancy exceeds two months, its notification and record are regularly published by this department.

This department was established with two objectives: to check the growth of population, and to prevent the chronically ill and those with hereditary diseases from producing offspring. Both objectives have been fully achieved. The reason why nowadays not a single person afflicted with leprosy, epilepsy, syphilis, hemorrhoids, and such diseases is found, is precisely due to these efforts. Patients suffering from such contagious diseases are first separated from the general public and kept comfortably, and their treatment is thoroughly arranged. In this way, they are not given the opportunity to spread the disease through contact. Secondly, to ensure that they do not have offspring, their reproductive capacity is destroyed by specially prescribed methods. In this manner, these diseases, the age-old enemies of the human race, have been eradicated.

Even so, it was observed that if no restrictions were imposed, the human population would continue to increase uncontrollably. Committees of experts calculated the average annual income of the Earth and reported their findings. It was determined that only a little more than one and three-quarter billion people could live a happy life on this basis. What followed? It was also calculated how many births would be needed to replace the number of deaths, and how many would constitute actual growth. If every married couple had only two children, then...

If each couple produces only three children, this increase can be checked. For this, once again, the same process of destroying reproductive power was put into practice. Now, since the responsibility for the comfort of every man and woman in their old age lies with the nation, the intense desire to have children has already diminished. And through this process, only the reproductive power is reduced; everything else remains as before. For this reason, people themselves prefer it. Earlier, many men opposed it. They argued that population growth must certainly be checked, but not by artificial means—rather, through self-restraint and discipline. Those of another view said that such self-restraint is not an easy task, one that the entire nation can follow. If that is the case, then to relax on this matter is, in a way, to encourage population growth itself. The nation cannot afford to leave its needs unfulfilled, relying on this mirage. Thus, the result now is that, just like other matters, the increase or decrease of the population is in the hands of the nation’s leaders, just as turning electric lights on and off is.

After residing in Nalanda for a full fortnight, I began my next journey. Vishwamitra was thoroughly acquainted with both the present and the past worlds, and he had also become well acquainted with me. Therefore, I chose him as my companion for the journey. He too accepted this very gladly. On our way here, although we had passed through Patna, it was nighttime and we could not disembark, so we learned nothing about it. Now, for our onward journey, it was decided that our first stop from Nalanda would be Patna. As we traveled during the day, the scenes along the way were clearly visible. Vishwamitra was familiar with the villages in this area. From time to time, he would tell me much about the villages we passed. The distance from Nalanda to Patna by ordinary train is two hours.

chapters.title: Departure from Nalanda
paragraphs: On the way, we saw many mango orchards. I said to Vishwamitra, “The Malda and Langda mangoes of Patna were already very famous.” He replied, “Now, both their size and flavor have improved even further. The mangoes from here are sent all over the world, from Sumeru (the North Pole) to Kumeru (the South Pole). Videha, Magadha, and Anga—these three regions are the world’s orchards for mangoes and lychees. A great portion of their land and inhabitants are devoted to their cultivation. The remarkable thing is that now both these fruits are available all twelve months of the year. At any time, thousands of trains, loaded with these fruits and preserved with ice, race toward various parts of Asia and Europe. The railway network is so dense that, except for Australia and some island groups, it covers the entire globe.

From Kathmandu (Nepal), Darjeeling, and Sadiya, three routes cross the Himalayas, and the railway has entered Tibet. The railway stretches far into Tibet now. The old squalor among the Tibetan people is no more. In fact, now no child of humanity anywhere on earth is deprived of cleanliness or the virtues of civilized man. Education and the means of happiness are distributed to all as needed. From Tibet, the railway line, weaving its way through Mongolia, crosses the Altai Mountains and reaches Siberia. From Mongolia, railways extend into various provinces of Manchuria and China, and then, passing through Yunnan, spread into Siam and Burma. Burma is now connected by rail to Chittagong and the Assam province. Not only that, but from Burma, passing through Malaya, a tunnel under the sea connects Singapore and Sumatra as well.

From Tibet westward, the railway network stretches through Yarkand and Kashgar in Turkestan, then to Tashkent, Samarkand, and onward to Afghanistan, Iran, Turkey, and Arabia. The railways have entered Russia by crossing the Ural Mountains at several points. Here, at Constantinople, tunnels under the seas have joined Asia and Europe. Between France and England too, railways with tunnels beneath the sea have been laid. The tunnel-railway of the Suez Canal has joined Asia and Africa. In Africa...

Everywhere, too, there is a network of railways. In recent centuries, the wondrous feat has been accomplished of filling the sandy expanse of the Sahara with an immense body of water, creating a sea, and transforming millions of miles of surrounding desert into lush greenery. The population of Africa has also increased greatly. Half of Europe has migrated there, and, in addition, many people from Asia have also settled in those lands. But now, those old distinctions of race and nation are gone. All live together as one family. Africans, Europeans, and Asians are equal in education and upbringing, and even in complexion and other traits, they are becoming more and more alike. Thus, the railway lines are spread across the eastern hemisphere. From Siberia, trains pass through a tunnel beneath the Bering Strait and reach Alaska, in northern America. From there, they run through Canada, the United States, and Mexico, crossing the Panama Canal by tunnel, and enter South America, spreading out across Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Patagonia, and all the other regions. Although, in this way, nearly the entire earth—leaving aside Australia, some smaller islands, and Japan—has been connected by railways, ships still play a major role in transporting goods with ease. Besides these, long-distance journeys are made by aircraft. Settlements have sprung up at the main northern and southern poles, where people reside during the warm or six-month-long days. Experts in astronomy and physical sciences gather there in greater numbers. Travel is by air. People today may well read tales of Scott’s self-sacrifice, but can they truly comprehend the hardships of those times? As we journeyed through Magadh and Patna, these topics arose in conversation. For this, Magadh is known for its mangoes and lychees. Passing through these endless orchards of mangoes and lychees, we finally reached Patna. News of our arrival had already been sent ahead. The president of the Magadh Administrative Assembly, our comrade Yusuf, along with several other members, had come to the station to welcome us. Regarding the welcome...

I wish to state, once and for all, that every locality strove to outdo the others. When I beheld the city, it became clear that not only was Pataliputra a thing apart, but even Patna’s former appearance had been utterly transformed. The entire city of Patna now houses only fifteen thousand people. Those cramped lanes and streets have vanished without a trace, and there is no sign of the old multi-storied buildings. All the dwellings resemble those of villages. There is the same fondness for flower gardens and trees. Thus, where once a thousand people lived, now scarcely fifty to a hundred reside.

Patna is the capital of the Magadh Republic. Many national offices are located here. The printing press is immense. There is a major wireless telegraph station. The airfield is also a large hub. The principal occupation of all the residents here is to work in these departments. Although all the houses are single-storied, the offices themselves rise to several floors. The record office, which houses all the documents, is a full fifty stories high. Ascending from the bottom to the topmost floor is a laborious task; therefore, an electric elevator is provided for moving up and down. In this office, every document of the nation is preserved with great care. There are thorough measures to protect the papers from fire and other dangers. This office contains not only documents from the English rule pertaining to Magadh, but also many decrees and records from the Muslim era have been collected. The most beautiful building in Patna is Ashoka Bhavan. Its design is modeled after the Vasubandhu Bhavan of Nalanda, but its splendor surpasses even that. One can see exquisite work in gold and marble throughout. Its size matches that of the Vasubandhu Bhavan. Above the stage, in large golden letters, is inscribed: “Eṣa ca mukha bhūte vijaye devanāṁ priyasa yo bhrama vijayo.”
Departing from Patna, although I spent two or four days in each of the present republics of India, the settlements and ways of living everywhere were much the same.

I observed. Although I have been recording in my daily journal the details of the things around me, I shall refrain from quoting them here, considering it mere repetition. Instead, I will offer only a brief account of the major changes I encountered in the course of my travels.

Leaving behind the Magadh Republic along with Patna, I proceeded to Banaras, the city of the Kashi Republic. Banaras, too, has undergone great transformations. It is neither the old Kashi Karwat nor the Kachauri Gali, nor its famed kachauris. The very names of those narrow lanes have vanished. In their place are wide, spacious roads. The houses, standing in open, airy spaces, possess the same elegance as previously described. If, today, someone were to search for a house from the twentieth century, they would not find it. I felt an even deeper melancholy when I visited Manikarnika, Dashashwamedh, and other once-crowded ghats of old. Though, even now, many bathers come at bathing times, and the steps are more beautiful and clean than ever before; some boats, powered by electricity, can be seen swiftly gliding across the Ganges—yet where is the bustle of the ghats and the priests? Where is that constant chant of “guru-guru,” the scraping of the wooden sticks and the clatter of the baskets? There is no sign of the barbers or the gardeners. How could there be, when even the very notion of money itself has disappeared—where, then, would their followers find a place? There is no longer the Satti of Dashashwamedh, nor the granaries of Visheshwarganj; no trace of the bulls and the unruly crowds. Gone, too, are the brothels of Dalmandi, where the unfortunate women, victims of the society of that era, once lived. The houses where people dwell are all single-storied. Around every historic site, lush, green, open spaces are to be seen.

The temples are now preserved as historical monuments. There is no longer any need to manage offerings of money. At present, only twenty-five thousand men and women reside in all of Banaras—if the old houses still stood, they would fit into a single corner, but thanks to the broad roads, single-storied houses, and the abundance of flowers and greenery, the population is spread across the entire expanse of old Banaras.
Near Banaras, there are two other famous settlements. One is Barna, and three kos beyond, across the river, is “Rishipatan Mrigadava”—which was once called Sarnath—ten thousand...

chapters.title: The Democracies of India
paragraphs: There is a settlement of people here. Guest-rest houses have been built far and wide. The Buddhists hold this place in great reverence, for it was here that the Buddha first delivered his teachings. Men and women from all over the globe come here. The place has now become exceedingly beautiful. The old, nearly ruined stupas have been completely rebuilt. The second notable place is Assi, across from the Kashi Vishwavidyalaya (Benares Hindu University). Its expanse now stretches much farther than before. The old schools and the home-schools of the pandits no longer exist, yet this has not caused any decline in the spread of learning. The study and teaching of all disciplines are now conducted in the Kashi Vishwavidyalaya in a manner even more systematic than before. It is counted among the highest-ranking universities of the world. It is especially renowned for its literature and philosophy.

The capital of the Kashi province is Banaras. Wheat cultivation and the orchards of mango, guava, and jujube are abundant here. Especially in the district of Banaras, the aforementioned fruits are found in great quantity.
In addition, a great deal of sugar is produced in this province. The number of canals has increased since earlier times, but the population has decreased.

Indraprastha, Vatsa, Panchala, Surasena, Matsya, and Kuru are independent republics. Many of the principalities from the twentieth century are now included within Surasena and Matsya. There remains no trace of those former principalities. The capital of India is Delhi; however, the city itself has a population of only fifty thousand. In cleanliness and beauty, it has greatly surpassed its former state. The old buildings are preserved in excellent condition. Wheat, sugar, and ghee are sent from here to other places as well. Towards the Terai region, there are many villages dedicated to paper-making.

In Punjab and Kashmir, too, there are many democracies. The capital of one is Lahore. The Takshashila University has regained its ancient glory. Its fame in the science of Ayurveda is spread throughout the world. Besides wheat, other grains, and sugar, this land produces a great quantity of dried fruits. In the northern mountainous regions, there are many villages of shepherds. There are many large factories for woolen cloth. In this region as well, there are many places for the generation of electricity.
Rajasthan. In this are included all the lands of the former Rajput principalities.

The greatest transformation, apart from the unification of numerous principalities, is the conversion of the desert into lush green plains. The great canal of Sindh, by cooling the parched, sand-burnt heart of Bikaner that once thirsted for water, has brought about this change. Ajmer is its capital.

Sindh. The produce here is abundant in both fruits and grains. The capital is Karachi, a major hub for both ships and aircraft. From here, I traveled to Saurashtra, Gujarat, Malwa, Vidarbha, and Maharashtra. In all three, cotton is cultivated extensively. There are many large textile mills. The old Hyderabad principality has now been divided into four republics: North Maharashtra, South Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Andhra. In these provinces too, cotton and textile mills abound. However, the production of rice and sugar is also significant. Besides Dravid and Kerala, Lanka too is now included within India. In addition to these, Utkal, Bengal, Assam, and the Himalayan states are all part of India. The administration and condition of all these places are exceptionally beautiful. The inhabitants are joyful, and the earth is bountiful. Everywhere, there are numerous schools and universities.

Previously, there was a rampant obsession with becoming wealthy by any means. At that time, people also had the freedom to do so. The value of any commodity was not determined by national necessity. The wealthy, driven by the desire for riches, hardly cared whether a particular trade would ruin the nation’s labor and life, or prove meaningful. They only observed what was in demand in the market. For that alone, they would open vast factories, employing hundreds of thousands of people. Alcohol, cigarettes, and opium—though all harmful substances—still claimed the labor of hundreds of thousands of people and occupied hundreds of thousands of acres of land for their production.

chapters.title: Things That Have Disappeared from the Present World
paragraphs: used to exist. But how could such things be tolerated nowadays? Here, the principle is firmly established: all the necessary, harmless, and pleasurable materials of life should be collected in sufficient quantity with as little time spent as possible, so that people may devote the remaining time to pursuits of their own choosing, to works that they desire. In earlier times, vast tracts of land in the Darbhanga and Muzaffarpur districts were given over to the cultivation of tobacco, but now there is no trace of tobacco there. The factories of cigars, cigarettes, and bidis are nowhere to be found. Not only alcohol and opium, but also hemp, bhang, charas, toddy, and many such substances can now only be read about or seen in museums of objects. Tea, coffee, and kahwa too have been dismissed as useless addictions.

Since there is no distinction between high and low in food, inferior grains such as sawan, kodon, mandua (ragi), coarse rice, and so on are no longer cultivated. The fruits and grains that are produced for consumption are all of the finest quality. The same holds true for clothing, dwellings, conveyances, and hospitality.

With the disappearance of money and the abolition of private property, fruits and flowers, fields and orchards, factories and workshops—all are now national property; and for this reason, there is no longer the proliferation of laws as before. The laws of income tax, land settlement, court fees, excise, tenancy, rent, joint-stock companies, and hundreds of others are now obsolete. The very root of civil litigation has vanished, for no individual owns wealth or land. The scope of criminal law has also greatly diminished, since crimes such as theft and robbery for the sake of property are no longer possible. The motive for one person to cause physical or mental harm to another remains only in name, for the root of all these was individual ownership. The excellent organization of education, the advanced treatment of diseases, the birth of healthy and robust children to healthy parents—these are the factors, the very corners from which, in earlier times, so many crimes used to arise, but today, crime is either absent or nearly so.

Now, there are only two main causes of crime: the occasional turbulence of human nature and ignorance, and the relations between men and women. But even these, compared to earlier times, are not a hundredth as—

Reconciliations are not possible; the reason is—a profound transformation has taken place in human nature, and men and women are now regarded as absolutely equal. Today, a man has no more rights over a woman than a woman has over a man. Both are bound only by the ties of love. Just as the marital bond is held together solely by love, so too is it considered stable only as long as that love endures. In the absence of love, this bond is entirely dissolved. When neither husband nor wife is economically dependent on the other, when there is no fear of social opposition, then how long, and for how many days, can they continue to pretend to be a married couple? One consequence of this is that secret adultery, as was common before, has greatly diminished.

In today’s world, many professions no longer exist. Not only are there no lawyers, attorneys, solicitors, or barristers; there are also no cobblers, sweepers, prostitutes, beggars, priests, bards, caretakers of shrines, butchers, shopkeepers, and so on. There are no servants, maids, or masters either. Child marriage and mismatched marriages are unheard of. There is no trace of dowries, pageantry, grand wedding processions, elephants, horses, palanquins, fireworks, or any such things. The rituals and sacrifices to gods and saints, offerings, and animal sacrifices have all disappeared. There is no caste discrimination, no color prejudice. Hereditary diseases and royal ailments—leprosy, asthma, piles, insanity, tuberculosis, syphilis, and the like—are no longer heard of. In the previous century, the nation had to wage a great battle against these diseases before victory was achieved. All such patients—both men and women—were rendered incapable of reproduction through medical procedures and were segregated. This task was extremely difficult and was not accomplished all at once. But once the nation understood what was in its best interest and resolved to act, how could the work remain undone? It is the result of the nation’s efforts that now, on earth, one cannot find blind, lame, crippled, deaf, mute, one-eyed, feeble-minded, or sensory-deformed individuals.
